We were off to the races. I immediately cast about to find some means of dislodging the boss. My first solution was simple: plunge the realm in an internecine civil war that scourges the land with blood and fire. Unfortunately, I soon realised I probably wouldn't be allowed to suggest that as an option for the American people in an international videogames publication, so I decided to, like, win an election or something instead. Whatever.

Well, okay, not just win an election. The bloodless paths to power I saw were to either get myself nominated as the old man's heir (HRE elections aren't as regular as modern-day America's—at the time of writing—and so I couldn't replace him directly via one) or to butter him up so nicely that he declares me co-ruler.

I opted for both. My first move was to ply my delicate kaiser with flattery and gifts. He liked flattery and gifts, and as a bonus, by showering him with them I significantly decreased the odds I would wake up to find all my lands redistributed among his wretched children. I increased the odds I would wake up at all, at that.

With my other hand, I penned fawning letters to his most powerful vassals: 'My esteemed lord, my honourable lady, your most munificent worshipfulness…' On and on I went, doling out what little gifts were available to me, and starting schemes to sway and cajole the realm's most powerful. It all seemed, almost boringly, to be coming together. Perhaps the great secret to overcoming your political enemies is… just being plain old nice?

No. Absolutely not. Being nice is just the vague flouncing about you do before you get serious and start organising the guillotines. Though I had successfully gotten a fair few influential figures on-side, none of them seemed inclined to support me for the big chair. As for Wenzel? He was fond of me, but he was also ancient and deranged, and was apparently too busy getting deep into religious superstition (quite literally, he acquired the 'superstition' modifier while I wasn't looking, somehow) to dedicate much thought to power sharing.
Time to get serious.
Not time to get serious

Somehow this goddamn idiot caused a plague. I don't know how, I don't know why, I don't know if what I am describing is even really possible within the mechanics of Crusader Kings 3, but our awful pervert king caused a plague and proceeded to ravage my counties with it. This is what happened regardless as to whether it's possible or not.

It was called "Wenzel's Cough" and it quickly tore through most of my subjects (eh) and my entire family (uh oh). My wife had it, my daughters had it, my sons had it, I had it. The whole castle probably looked like a boss arena from Hunt: Showdown—walls caked in viscous emissions and baking like an orchid hothouse.

The busywork of not dying distracted me from the quest to depose Wenzel. I isolated the capital and secured a personal physician, whom I oriented in the general direction of my family and said "Just go nuts chief." He locked me in a room with a trillion bees (this actually happened), which somehow gave major relief to my consumption. I lost the ominous 'Dying' warning at the top of the screen and was free to return to politics. Most of my family got relief too, save one son who died. Fortunately, it was one I was mostly unaware of up to that point.

With my attempts at diplomacy foiled, I figured it was time to try war. Wenzel had about 7,000 men in his army whereas I had 1,400. Defeating him on the battlefield would need allies. I began a scheme to sway one of his most powerful vassals: a Tuscan duchess named Matilda with a decent army. Perhaps I could marry her? My current wife was an obstacle, true, but an obstacle with a boutique variant of tuberculosis, so it might all work itself out.
At some point while all this was happening, Wenzel developed the traits "Irritable" and "Withering mind."
And then this idiot duchess went and declared a war of independence against Wenzel without me, practically guaranteeing her defeat, imprisonment, and possible execution.

What's the real-life lesson here? You can't rely on the tender feelings of powerful people to hand you your salvation in dark political times. They have their own stupid ends and will pursue them to your detriment.

You also can't rely on your loved ones to die from plague at times that are convenient to you, so my plan might not have worked even if Matilda hadn't gone war-mode. Sometime after our Tuscan duchess declared war, Wenzel's cough abated in my lands. The city gates swung open again, and the cloud of death lifted from over my realm.

Except for me, of course. Despite my physician's daring bee treatment, my condition had worsened to the point that the 'Dying' notification was back. Even more galling: I kept proccing events that showed every individual member of my family recovering fully from the disease, one by one. "The sound of laughter echoes in your halls again," beamed CK3, as a new notification asked if I wanted to have my last rites performed or if I wanted to go to hell.

Idiot Matilda lost her war around the time I choked out my last on my deathbed, surrounded by my family who were all absolutely fine. In the imperial capital, Wenzel tottered along, muttering to himself as he roamed cavernous palatial spaces. He had new traits: high blood pressure and a faulty heart, but refused to die. A new plague was working its way north through the world towards him. He refused to die. An exploding heart, deranged mind, and multiple competing plagues, and he refused to die.
I died, though, having not figured out how to remove a senile moron from power. Well, good luck America.

One of Josh's first memories is of playing Quake 2 on the family computer when he was much too young to be doing that, and he's been irreparably game-brained ever since. His writing has been featured in Vice, Fanbyte, and the Financial Times. He'll play pretty much anything, and has written far too much on everything from visual novels to Assassin's Creed. His most profound loves are for CRPGs, immersive sims, and any game whose ambition outstrips its budget. He thinks you're all far too mean about Deus Ex: Invisible War.

articles.headline: Reported attacks on ships around Strait of Hormuz reach record highs
keyFacts: The U.K. Maritime Trade Operations monitoring agency said reported attacks on vessels in or near the Strait of Hormuz reached a weekly high of at least ten.
Saudi strikes killed 12 people in Yemen, and the Saudi-led coalition intercepted four drones over Saudi territory, according to Houthi media and the coalition.
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi stated that Egypt was ready to defend Saudi Arabia if requested by the kingdom.
body: What to know about the Iran war today:

- The U.K. Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) monitoring agency said at least ten vessels have been attacked in or near the Strait of Hormuz since last Sunday, a weekly high since war broke out in February, and 23 attacks were recorded since the start of the month, almost double the average.
- Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian denied Friday that Tehran sought nuclear weapons, expressed readiness for dialogue and condemned U.S. sanctions during talks with Georgia's prime minister.
- The Strait of Hormuz will reopen if the U.S. leaves the Middle East, a spokesman for 's army said Friday. "If it does not leave, we will expel it," Mohammad Akraminia wrote on X.
Iranian foreign minister meets with several Middle East counterparts at regional gathering

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, one of the leading members of past negotiations with the United States, met with a handful of his counterparts on Saturday at a gathering of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation in Baghdad.

Among those he met was Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan even as Turkey is part of a trilateral cooperation agreement with Pakistan and Saudi Arabia, which is coming under fire from the Iran-backed Houthi militia.
The two sides discussed "the latest developments in Palestine and Yemen, emphasizing diplomatic efforts to reduce tensions," according to the Iranian government.

"During the bilateral talks, FM Araghchi also reviewed the latest developments in the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz, briefing his Turkish counterpart on ongoing diplomatic trends and emphasizing Islamic cooperation to face shared regional challenges," the Iranian government said on X.
Araghchi also met with foreign leaders from Egypt, which said Saturday it would defend Saudi Arabia from Houthi attacks; Libya; Lebanon; and Algeria.
Saudi strikes on Yemen kill 12, Iran-backed Houthis say
Saudi strikes that began overnight have killed at least 12 people in Yemen, three of them children, Houthi media reported on Saturday.

Saudi warplanes targeted "civilian homes" in Taiz governorate on Saturday, killing nine people and wounding 16, the Iran-backed group's news agency said, adding people were still trapped under the rubble.
The agency had earlier reported overnight strikes in Dhamar province that killed three children and wounded 17 other people.
It said the strikes were carried out "using cluster bombs, which are banned internationally."
The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis has launched daily raids in Yemen backing the internationally recognized government in the country's long-running civil war.
Saudis intercept 4 drones over country in recent hours
The Saudi-led coalition fighting against the Iran-backed Houthis have intercepted four drones over Saudi territory in the last few hours, the group said.
The drones were intercepted over the capital city of Riyadh, and in the Eastern, and Southern regions, according to the coalition.
The Houthis have regularly launched drones and missiles at the Saudis every day for the last several weeks.

The coalition announced overnight it had taken out two missile-launch platforms in the Saada Governorate, which is the northern-most region in Yemen and controlled by the Houthis. A missile launch one week ago hit King Khallid International Airport in Riyadh and killed 13 people.
President Sisi says Egypt ready to defend Saudi Arabia "if requested"
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi on Saturday said Egypt was ready to defend Saudi Arabia "if requested," as fighting flares between the kingdom and Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen.

Since Yemen's war reignited in July, the Houthis have repeatedly attacked Saudi targets, including energy facilities and Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport, where 13 people were killed in a single attack last Saturday.
The Houthis have also blockaded the Bab el-Mandeb Strait to Saudi-flagged tankers, piling pressure on energy exports as Iran presses its own blockade on the Strait of Hormuz.

Speaking at a graduation ceremony at the Egyptian military academy, Sisi said Egypt was "not looking for a role to play" in regional conflicts, but added it was "inconceivable" for Cairo to stand by while Saudi Arabia was "harmed or its security and stability threatened."
"Egypt, of course, with the directives of His Majesty King Salman and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, will carry out any measure to protect you or defend you," he said.
He added any deployment would require parliamentary approval and said he hoped lawmakers would convene in an emergency session to grant authorization "if it is requested of us."
"I'm not talking about fighting anyone or attacking anyone," Sisi said. "We are speaking only about defense."
Yemen's Houthis free 159 pro-government fighters under amnesty
Yemen's Houthis on Saturday announced the release of 159 pro-government fighters under an amnesty announced after they seized swathes of land in a major offensive last month.

The prisoners had "voluntarily surrendered themselves without fighting" as the Iran-backed group captured strategic positions along the Red Sea, Houthi official Abdelqader al-Murtada told a press conference in Sanaa.

The Houthis' war with the Saudi-backed, internationally recognized government reignited in July after four years of calm, triggering attacks on Saudi oil shipments and other targets including airports.

The International Committee of the Red Cross confirmed the unilateral release of 159 prisoners and said it had given support by organizing interviews and health checks, contacting families and helping arrange transport.
Murtada said 323 prisoners were released under the amnesty last month after surrendering in Hodeidah governorate.
Iran backs "political process" to resolve Saudi-Houthi conflict, foreign minister says
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Saturday that Tehran supports a "political process" to resolve the conflict between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis.
The Houthis have repeatedly attacked Saudi targets, including energy facilities and Riyadh's international airport, where 13 people were killed in a major attack one week ago.

"We support an inclusive and comprehensive political process as the only practical and sustainable way to resolve the issue," Araghchi said in a speech at the Organization of Islamic Cooperation in Baghdad.
Araghchi repeated Iran's offer to mediate between the two sides. Deputy Foreign Minister Saeed Khatibzadeh previously said Riyadh has not responded to Iran's overture.
On Friday, Iran denied having anything to do with the Houthi attacks, after Saudi Arabia accused Tehran of encouraging the group's escalation.

In his speech, Araghchi also said "either we build security together, or we will endure insecurity together," adding Tehran was willing "to cooperate with all its brothers and neighbours to achieve the first option."
The Houthis in Yemen and Hezbollah in Lebanon are part of Iran's "Axis of Resistance" against Israel and the United States, which also includes armed groups in Iraq.
Oil tanker reportedly hits mine in Strait of Hormuz
Iran's Revolutionary Guards Corps on Saturday said an oil tanker was on fire in the Strait of Hormuz after hitting a mine in the waterway at the heart of the Middle East war.

"A supertanker in violation of regulations, carrying more than two million barrels of crude oil and attempting to pass illegally through the Strait of Hormuz, struck a mine, triggering an explosion and a fierce fire," the Iranian military said.
The statement did not specify the exact location of the incident.
"The tanker attempted to cross the strait with U.S. support... by deactivating all its tracking systems," the Guards added, also posting a video of a vessel in flames during the night.
Ship attacked by RPG fired from small boat, British maritime agency said
The U.K. Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) monitoring agency reported on Saturday a second attack on a ship off the coast of Saudi Arabia, which took place a day early.
In a post on social media, the UKMTO said: "The master of a tanker has reported being attacked by an RPG (rocket-propelled grenade) from a small boat, resulting in damage to the aft port quarter."
Friday's attack is the second reported by the agency on that day off the coast of Al Jubayl in Saudi Arabia.
"Crew are accounted for and reported safe," the UKMTO said, but the full extent of the damage and environmental impact were not known at the time of the report.
Ship struck by "unknown projectile" off the coast of Saudi Arabia, maritime agency says
A British maritime agency said Saturday it had received a report of a vessel struck on the Persian Gulf on Friday.
The U.K. Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said the tanker had been struck by an "unknown projectile" off the coast of Saudi Arabia.
"All crew are reported safe and have been evacuated. There is no reported environmental impact at the time of report," the statement added.
The UKMTO had previously reported that October had become the busiest month for reported attacks on ships in the Strait Hormuz.
Reported shipping attacks jump in Strait of Hormuz, British monitor says
A British monitor says October has become the busiest month for reported attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz since March, during the Iran war's opening months.
That's as the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations said it was "struggling to accurately report" the true number of attacks since most ships now refuse to report them.

Still, UKMTO said 10 attacks were reported in the week ending Friday. One ship sank. Since early July, most attacks have occurred off Oman, where the U.S. military has been guiding vessels at risk of Iranian attack.
There has been an uptick in attacks since President Trump late last month rejected a Tehran proposal to end the war and open the strait, though indirect negotiations have continued.
2 missiles strike airport in Yemen's port city of Aden, officials say
Two missiles struck the airport in Yemen's port city of Aden on Friday night, police said, blaming Iran-backed Houthi rebels for the second such attack in less than a week.

Police said no casualties were reported as fighting escalates in the latest front in the Iran war, one in which the rebels have attacked both neighboring Saudi Arabia and Yemen's internationally recognized government that's backed by the kingdom.

A security official and a traffic controller told The Associated Press an area of the Aden airport that hosts a military unit aligned with the Saudi-backed government was hit. Both spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to the media.
There was no immediate claim of responsibility.
Iran denies Saudi accusation of involvement in Houthi attacks
Iran's foreign ministry on Friday rejected Saudi Arabia's accusation that Tehran was involved in Houthi attacks on the kingdom, offering to mediate between the two sides.

"The Islamic Republic of Iran rejects any claim that Iran has played a role in Yemeni (Houthi) operations," Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei said in a statement, reiterating Tehran's offer to act as a bridge between the Houthis and Riyadh.
Regardless of how involved Iran has been in Houthi attacks, the .
They were once a relatively marginal group within what Iran calls its — a loose alliance of anti-Israel, anti-U.S. militant groups that includes Hamas in Gaza and Hezbollah in Lebanon.

"The Houthis are the most powerful proxy within the Iranian network, hands down," said Mohammed Al-Basha, founder of the Basha Report, a U.S.-based risk advisory group. "Any U.S. military strategy planning a campaign on Iran will have to take into consideration what the Houthis will do next."
Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia have killed about 20 people in the last several weeks, including 13 in one strike on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport last weekend.
CBS/AFP
Iran's president denies nuclear ambitions, says country ready for talks
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian denied Friday that Tehran sought nuclear weapons, expressed readiness for dialogue and condemned U.S. sanctions during talks with Georgia's prime minister.

In his meeting with Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze, Pezeshkian also called for closer ties with Georgia, weeks after Tbilisi cut aviation links between the two countries following U.S. sanctions targeting Iranian airlines.
The two met on the sidelines of a U.N. biodiversity summit in Armenia's capital, Yerevan.
"Iran is not seeking nuclear weapons, and we consider the malicious propaganda against our country to be lies," Pezeshkian said, according to a statement from his office.
"We have always been ready for dialogue. They think they can force us to surrender, but we will not bow to coercion," he added, calling U.S. sanctions against Tehran "unjustifiable and inhumane."
Georgia's Civil Aviation Agency said in September it would comply with U.S. sanctions, while Kobakhidze insisted Tbilisi was not imposing its own bilateral sanctions on Tehran.
Saudi-hosted Asian Cup soccer tournament remains on schedule despite Houthi attacks

Asian Cup organizers insisted Friday the continental soccer championship set to be held in Saudi Arabia in early 2027 remains on track despite a wave of missile and drone attacks on the host country in recent days.
The Saudi organizing committee issued a statement Friday saying it is continuing to coordinate closely with the Asian Football Confederation. The tournament is scheduled for Jan. 7 to Feb. 5.

"Preparations across all organizational and operational areas are progressing according to the approved schedule, including work on venues, facilities and supporting services," Saudi organizers said. "The focus remains on delivering a world-class tournament experience for participating teams, fans and media from across Asia, while bringing the continent together through football."
South Korea's Professional Footballers' Association had earlier expressed concerns following a series of attacks on the Asian Cup host country by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels.

"The continued military tensions and security instability in the Middle East are issues that can never be taken lightly," Lee Keun-ho, head of the South Korean player union, said in a statement. "The safety of our national team, as well as all players participating in the Asian Cup, is a serious concern."

At least 19 people, including foreigners, have been killed in more than a week of Houthi attacks targeting the Riyadh international airport, the headquarters of Saudi oil giant Aramco and other aviation, oil and military facilities across the kingdom.

Several sporting events have already been canceled or postponed in Saudi Arabia, including Netflix's Six Kings Slam tennis tournament; women's tennis' WTA Finals, which were moved to the U.S.; multiple matches for the Saudi soccer club Al-Nassr, which features Cristiano Ronaldo; and an Olympic qualifying event for BMX cycling.
AP/CBS
Attacks on Yemen government palace compound killed 5, officials say
Attacks on the palace compound of Yemen's internationally recognized government Thursday killed at least five people and wounded more than a dozen others, government officials said.
In a Facebook post late Thursday, Health Minister Qasem Buhaibeh said security guards and other employees at Maashiq palace in Yemen's southern port city of Aden were among the casualties.

Aden has been the seat of Yemen's government since 2015. The Houthis claimed responsibility for the attacks, saying they targeted a military operations headquarters associated with Saudi forces backing the government.
Two of the missiles launched by the Houthis on Thursday struck near the headquarters of the Saudi-backed coalition forces in Aden, causing damage, a Yemeni government official said.

The official, speaking on condition of anonymity because he wasn't authorized to speak to the media, said Friday the missiles landed near the compound used by the coalition in Buraiqah, a neighborhood west of the palace. No senior officials were there at the time of the attack, he said.
Saudi-led coalition intercepts missiles and drones

Saudi-led coalition spokesperson Maj. Gen. Turki Al-Maliki announced a series of interceptions in successive X posts on Friday, saying Saudi forces had destroyed a ballistic missile, two cruise missiles and three drones over Saudi Arabia or the Red Sea.
In a first tweet, Al-Maliki said coalition forces intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched toward Yanbu.
A second post announced the interception and destruction of two cruise missiles over the Red Sea.
He then reported three drones had been intercepted and destroyed in Saudi Arabia's southern region and the Riyadh region.
Iraq says Iran war has deprived it of $60 billion in oil export revenue
Iraq has lost around $60 billion during the U.S.-Iran war, Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein said Thursday, as the fighting has blocked or severely impeded a waterway crucial to its oil exports.

OPEC member Iraq was producing about 4 million barrels of oil per day (bpd) before the conflict, and exporting about 3.5 million bpd – mostly carried by tankers out of the Persian Gulf via the Strait of Hormuz.

Iran's that fail to seek its permission to transit the strait has forced Iraq, which lacks sufficient storage capacity, to halt most production and fall back on limited exports via Syria and Turkey, by truck and pipeline respectively. Syria is set to provide an overland oil route to bypass the strait, the head of Syrian Petroleum Co. said last week.

"Iraq has suffered losses estimated at around $60 billion during the recent war between the United States and the Islamic Republic of Iran," Hussein told his Italian counterpart in Rome, according to a statement from the Iraqi foreign ministry.

After a heavy drop in production, Iraqi oil exports, which provide about 90% of the country's revenues, recovered modestly last month, reaching 2.6 million barrels per day between Sept. 1 and 21, according to the oil ministry. But at the same time, Iraq's foreign currency reserves have shrunk by $20 billion and consumer prices have risen sharply, plunging it into economic crisis.
CBS/AFP
Norwegian teen sentenced in U.K. to 20 years in prison for plotting murder for Iran-linked gang
A Norwegian teenager convicted of on behalf of an international crime gang linked to Iran was sentenced Friday to 20 years in prison.

Johannes Kongsnes Natland, 19, was found guilty in July of conspiracy to murder for agreeing to shoot someone unknown to him for $28,000 last year. He was arrested at a hotel in Huddersfield, in northern England, with two guns and ammunition two days after arriving in the U.K.

In bodycam video released by police from the early hours of March 19, 2025, Natland emerges topless from his room and mimes a shooting gesture at a firearms officer before being slammed against a wall.
It remains unknown who his intended target would have been.

Natland, who was working part time at a pizza restaurant at the time of his arrest, was recruited by a Swedish organized crime group known as the Foxtrot Network while he was playing a game online. The group has links to the Iranian government, according to London's counterterrorism police unit.

Natland was hired by a 17-year-old known as "Generalen." A court in Norway last year convicted the teenager of attempting to "contribute to murder" and sentenced him to 14 years in custody. A 16-year-old is awaiting trial in Norway for his role in the conspiracy.
CBS/AP
Iranian navy says a tanker is burning in the Gulf of Oman
The Iranian navy said Friday that it had identified a tanker on fire in what it called a prohibited area in the Gulf of Oman, east of the Strait of Hormuz.
The navy's public relations office said in a statement that military surveillance teams "discovered and identified a violating oil tanker that had caught fire in a prohibited area."
The vessel had "switched off its tracking systems and was attempting to pass through a prohibited area in the Gulf of Oman."

The navy did not say how the tanker "caught fire" but added that "the consequences of uncoordinated movements along routes and in prohibited areas are the creation of insecurity and serious hazards for other vessels."
At least three commercial vessels have been struck in the region in suspected Iranian attacks this week.
Iran says the Strait of Hormuz will reopen if the U.S. "leaves the region"
The Strait of Hormuz will reopen if the U.S. "leaves" the Middle East, an Iranian army official said Friday.

"If the United States leaves the region, the Strait of Hormuz will reopen and collective security will be established with the participation of the countries of the region, and the global economy will improve," army spokesman Mohammad Akraminia wrote on X. "If it does not leave, we will expel it."

He did not elaborate on whether he was calling for a withdrawal of military forces sent during the current war, all U.S. military forces across the region, or military and non-military U.S. government personnel.

Though there were credible reports earlier this month of oil exports from the Persian Gulf ramping back up to near pre-war levels, Iran and the U.S. continue offering conflicting narratives, with the Trump administration insisting the Strait of Hormuz is open, but Tehran claiming it is closed to all traffic unless Iranian authorities grant permission.

Greek maritime risk firm Marisks warned Thursday that ships continue to face "indiscriminate attacks," even if they turn off their tracking systems, which many ships have been doing to avoid detection.
Iran president says conflict in Mideast amounts to "ecocide"
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on Friday urged countries to condemn what he called "ecocide" in the Middle East caused by "wars of aggression" against his country.
Pezeshkian said the conflicts in Gaza and the wider Middle East had taken a significant toll on nature that extended beyond national borders and required "international solutions."

"What has occurred in our region as a result of wars of aggression is ecocide, or environmental genocide, and it must be condemned," Pezeshkian said at a nature summit in Armenia that was attended by United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres.
Pezeshkian decried an "atmosphere of distrust" between Iran and the U.S. in a recent interview with CBS News.

"As long as they don't cease doing what they're imposing on us every day, it's difficult to trust them," he said. "Every day, they increase the sanctions against us. Every day, they threaten us. Every day, they strike us, and they don't honor what they have put in writing. So, if they engage in talks, will they actually follow through?"
CBS/AFP
White House prepares plans to use weapon dubbed "mother of all bombs" on Iran, sources say
The White House and Pentagon have prepared plans to use a Massive Ordnance Air Blast bomb to hit military sites in Iran if ordered by President Trump, sources familiar with the matter told CBS News.

A Pentagon official told CBS News: "The Department of War plans for a wide range of operational scenarios to execute Presidential and Secretary level direction and to ensure mission success in any operational environment."

A White House spokesperson said: "We do not comment on sensitive military plans that may or may not exist. President Trump keeps all options on the table to ensure that Iran can never have a nuclear weapon."
Last week, Mr. Trump said the U.S. would not attack Iran before the midterm elections. He also touted "productive conversations" with Iran, though he did not provide specifics.
CNN first reported Thursday on the plans to use the Massive Ordnance Air Blast Bomb, or MOAB, on Iran.

Mr. Trump set a precedent for using the MOAB, also known as the "mother of all bombs," when it was used in 2017 to attack an Islamic State cave complex in Afghanistan. The bomb is the largest U.S. non-nuclear weapon, weighing upwards of 30,000 pounds at a cost of $170,000 per unit.

articles.headline: Romanian fighter jets shoot down 2 drones over Black Sea
keyFacts: Romanian F-16 fighter jets shot down two drones over the Black Sea after they illegally entered national airspace, the Defense Ministry said.
The origin of the drones was not immediately known, and the incident follows recent drone attacks on ships near Romania's coast.
NATO will discuss the issue at a North Atlantic Council meeting on Tuesday, according to Foreign Minister Oana Toiu.
body: Romanian F-16 fighter jets have shot down two drones over the country's territorial waters, according to the Romanian Defense Ministry.

"Two drones were engaged and shot down a few minutes ago by Romanian military pilots over the Black Sea, moments after they had illegally entered our country," Defense Minister Radu Miruta wrote on Facebook.
So far, no information has been released regarding the country of origin of the drones.
What do we know about the incident?
F-16 fighter jets shot down the drones some 20 kilometers (13 miles) southeast of Sulina.
"The first drone entered national airspace at 17:59 (14:59 GMT) and was shot down within two minutes," Miruta said.
He added that the second one was shot down at 6:05 p.m., five minutes after entering Romanian airspace.
"The Black Sea will be safe again," Romanian Foreign Minister Oana Toiu wrote on X. She added that NATO will discuss the issue at a North Atlantic Council meeting on Tuesday.
Drone attacks endanger navigation in the Black Sea
This drone incursion is the latest in a series of incidents believed to be a result of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
In October, several drone attacks on ships in the Black Sea were reported off the coasts of Romania and Bulgaria.
The most recent attack occurred on Thursday, when two chemical tankers were attacked off Romania's coast, leaving seven crew members missing.
Both vessels were anchored near the Sulina Canal, which connects the Danube River to the Black Sea. The canal serves as an export route for Ukraine.
Romania, an EU and NATO member, shares a 614-kilometer (381-mile) border with Ukraine, part of which is along the Danube.
The country has repeatedly reported Russian drone incursions into its airspace since Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Romania began shooting down these drones earlier this year.

articles.headline: Debra Wilson Also Confused On Why Games Keep Using Her Likeness
keyFacts: Actor Debra Wilson stated during a podcast that she lacks a firm explanation for why many video game characters share her real-world likeness.
Wilson expressed a preference for roles where characters do not resemble her so she can escape into the character.
Developers attribute her frequent digital appearances to her extensive experience and exceptional audition reels.
body: While I had always assumed it was the result of an airtight contract or a talent rep sent from heaven, it turns out Debra Wilson doesnât have a firm explanation as to why so many of her in-game performances feature her real-world likeness. During a podcast appearance, the prolific Wolfenstein, Wolverine, Suicide Squad, Star Wars Jedi and Death Stranding voice actor said the decision usually comes down to the developers.

“Honestly, I love games where they don’t look like me at all,” Wilson tells podcaster Joseph Shepherd. “I might as well just go and do theaterâ¦ If it just looks like me, then how do you get a chance to really escape into a character?”

While the episode of Hyperfixated was recorded before the release of Marvelâs Wolverine, the clip has recirculated, admittedly by some in bad faith. The MADtv star has been contributing vocal performances in games for decades, but itâs in recent history that a number of those digital roles share her uncanny appearance.

While she expresses confusion with Shepherd about her appearance as the one-eyed Morlock leader Callisto in Wolverine, Insomniac opted to have the primary cast resemble their stars, as was often the case with Call of Duty, Death Stranding and Star Wars Jedi. That said, her mirror imaged appearance as Amanda Waller in Suicide Squad: Kill the Justice League or Grace Walker in Wolfenstein isnât matched by any others.

After working on multiple games with this woman, I truly WISH you guys could see her casting audition videos compared to her competition. It's like watching 1996 Michael Jordan turn up to a high school basketball game. https://t.co/9h4MQD1VhH
— Del (@TheCartelDel) September 17, 2026

I think itâs amusing. Some level it to conspiracy theories. Developers in the field say her reappearances come down to a competition crushing reel, and that her years of experience show. “After working on multiple games with this woman, I truly WISH you guys could see her casting audition videos,” posted Del Walker, who worked on Jedi and Suicide Squad, the last time there was this fracas. “It’s like watching 1996 Michael Jordan turn up to a high school basketball game.”

Seeing character actors appear should always be cause for celebration. As the studio system collapses, many working, recognizable actors have been diversifying, popping up in more games than the ’90s FMV boom. Often studios want to make the most bang for their buck, ensuring Keanu rides co-pilot throughout Cyberpunk. Other times Jack Quaid is rigged to a slime cube for motion capture.

articles.headline: Enzo Maresca’s eerie prediction comes true as Man City boss makes Premier League history
keyFacts: Manchester City manager Enzo Maresca became the first manager in Premier League history to win his first seven matches in charge.
Phil Foden scored his first competitive goal since last December in a 3-2 win over Ipswich, fulfilling Maresca's prediction.
Erling Haaland and four other Manchester City players picked up knocks during the match.
body: Phil Foden helped Enzo Maresca create Premier League history after the Manchester City boss correctly backed him to break his goal drought.
Foden made an instant impact on his return to action following a three-match suspension by scoring his first competitive goal since last December in Saturday’s 3-2 win over Ipswich.
Phil Foden ended his barren spell in front of goal with City’s opener against Ipswich Getty
The 26-year-old opened the scoring for the Citizens from close range in the 19th minute following great work by Jeremy Doku.

It was a welcome strike for Foden, who has struggled to reach the levels he set in the 2023/24 season when he was crowned PFA Player of the Year after scoring 19 top-flight goals – 27 in all competitions.
While many wouldn’t have tipped Foden to get on the score sheet against the Tractor Boys, Maresca was in no doubt that his player would end his barren spell.
Speaking in his pre-match press conference on Friday, the Italian boldly predicted that Foden’s quality in front of goals would soon shine through.
What did Maresca say about Foden?
“He will score tomorrow!,” Maresca boldly predicted.
“We just try to work with him day by day.
“The international break and since the red card against United has been quite long.
“But he has been training well, he’s doing well since we made a very positive start, very good.
“We need to decide if he starts tomorrow or not and if he does, no doubt he will give us something.”
Foden’s goal would have delighted Maresca as his side continued their 100 per cent start to the season.
Maresca’s side bounced back following their 4-2 defeat to Paris Saint-Germain on Wednesday night
What Premier League record has Maresca created?
The victory gave Maresca a little taste of history by becoming the first manager in Premier League to win his first seven matches in charge of a club.
Erling Haaland scored twice to take his tally to eight goals in seven league games.
But there was concern for Maresca after the Norwegian was seen limping down the tunnel after the final whistle after taking a knock to his foot.
Haaland was expected to be rested for Tuesday’s Champions League clash with AEK Athens. with Maresca to now be hoping the striker is available for next weekend’s trip to Aston Villa .
But the injury concerns do not stop there for the Manchester City boss with a further four players picking up knocks.
Antoine Semenyo and Iliman Ndiaye were both seen limping after the match, while Mateo Kovacic and Matheus Nunes went off with knocks.
Erlign Haaland appeared in discomfort as he made his way down the tunnel at full time AFP
What did Foden say after ending his goal drought?
With his goal drought now over, Foden has declared his strike against Ipswich will be the catalyst for more in the ner future.

He told BBC Radio Manchester: “I set such high standards of myself to always try and score goals, assist, and because I hadn’t scored for a long time I’ve just been trying to practice as much as I can in training and hopefully it paid off.
“Today it finally did. I’m really happy. The first one is always the hardest to score.”
Foden also stated: “It’s been such a hard time.
“It’s been over a month I couldn’t play [due to suspension and international break], so it’s been quite annoying. I’ve had to be patient, train on my own sometimes, it’s not been easy.
“But today, to get out there and score and get three points, it’s what I’ve been thinking about for a long time.”
Foden will now be looking to reach double digits for goals for a seventh successive season Getty
Foden was also pressed for his opinion regarding the ongoing guilty verdict shrouding the club.
To which he said: “We just try to not listen to anything.
“ The noise going around, we try to just stick to our football, take it game by game, and I think you can see that it’s not affecting us one bit.
“ We’re still 100 per cent focussed on winning football games, and I think that’s how it has to be.
“ The main focus is doing our job, and that’s all we can do.”

articles.headline: As too much of the industry embrace their own death through genAI, Konami say it's real people that are most important for making good games
keyFacts: Konami Digital Entertainment president Hideki Hayakawa stated that generative AI will not bring significant changes to video game development.
Hayakawa said in Konami's latest integrated report that human creators and people are the most important factors in making entertaining games.
Hayakawa also mentioned that Konami provides systematic support to help creators understand, assess risks, and apply new technologies safely.
body: I've taken a habit, recently, to proclaim my desire to explode in lieu of anything more realistically violent I could wish upon myself when I feel stressed. And, in what would likely be more concerning if I were a sentient bomb talking to a bomb diffusal squad, I've been saying that a lot lately, primarily because of the copious amounts of AI nonsense I've been seeing… everywhere. Epic Games, the ever-boycottable company called Microsoft, the decompiling community, the poison has found its way into everyone's veins and it's making me want to, say it with me now, explode! So you can imagine my relief to hear a developer say they don't think AI will make a massive impact. The developer? Perhaps surprisingly, Konami.

Yes, yes, the same Konami we all rag on for equal parts valid and parasocial (Kojima will never acknowledge you, give it up) reasons. As spotted by Dengeki Online, and translated by Automaton, Konami Digital Entertainment president Hideki Hayakawa shared his thoughts on the rapid paced development of AI technology in the company's latest integrated report. Hayakawa, apparently, is going against the widespread belief that generative AI will make game development easier with his belief it won't bring a significant change, noting that "entry barriers have already been lowered by the advancements of generic game engines and the spread of UGC (user generated content)."

He said, "Even if AI use does lead to improvements in production efficiency, I believe that the most important factors in producing entertaining and innovative video games are people and creators." Hayakawa obviously isn't completely swearing off of it there, but crikey, it sure is refreshing to hear a company head have the tiniest bit of common sense when it comes to this whole debacle. Hayakawa further explained that the "kind of chemical reaction," that comes from developers with a range of backgrounds working together is "not something that can be easily replaced."

He did, also, in a very diplomatic fashion, also note that Konami does still want to generally support their developers when it comes to technological advancements. "Even when it comes to epoch-making technological innovations, Konami provides systematic support so that creators can get a grasp of new technologies, properly assess the risks they may bring, and safely apply them to game development," he said. Translation, it's always possible his tune changes, but at least there's something of a priority of getting real people to make games. I'll take it! My next request is the complete abolishment of AI in its totality. Maybe Konami isn't so suited for that task just yet.

articles.headline: 'Moderate' AG's office turned to groups that spent years suing prisons for recruiting help: emails reveal
keyFacts: Internal emails obtained by Fox News Digital show that Arizona Chief Deputy Attorney General Daniel Barr sought recruiting help from the ACLU and the Prison Law Office.
Barr asked the two left-wing legal groups for candidate recommendations to fill legal roles and general counsel positions for the Arizona Department of Corrections, Rehabilitation and Reentry.
The ACLU and the Prison Law Office have previously spent years suing the state corrections department and advocate substantial changes to incarceration policy.
body: EXCLUSIVE — Arizona Attorney General Kris Mayes’ office repeatedly sought recruiting help from two prominent left-wing legal groups that spent years suing the state’s corrections department alongside Mayes’ top deputy, internal emails obtained by Fox News Digital show.

Chief Deputy Attorney General Daniel Barr sought recommendations from the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) and Berkeley-based Prison Law Office (PLO) for attorneys to handle Arizona Department of Corrections, Rehabilitation and Reentry (ADCRR) work inside the Attorney General’s Office and later for candidates to serve as ADCRR general counsel, according to the emails.

Barr already had a long history with both groups before joining Mayes’ office. Prior to his position in the Arizona Attorney General’s Office , he was a partner at Perkins Coie, where he spent years litigating alongside the ACLU and PLO in a federal case that ultimately resulted in a judge finding Arizona’s prison conditions to be constitutionally inadequate .

Both groups advocate substantial changes to incarceration policy. The ACLU has pursued a nationwide goal of cutting jail and prison populations by 50% through reforms including decriminalization, bail reform, shorter sentences and clemency, and has called for reductions in immigration detention. The PLO, meanwhile, says it works to reduce incarceration while also litigating on issues related to prison conditions, medical care, disability rights and solitary confinement.
'THRILL KILLER' AND DESERT EXECUTIONER — MEET THE DOZENS OF CRIMINALS DEM AG BACKED FOR PAROLE: 'NO BRAINER'

In November's general election, Mayes is slated to face Arizona state Sen. Warren Petersen, a Republican, as she seeks to defend her role as the top law enforcement officer in the state. Mayes won her 2022 race by just 280 votes , one of the narrowest margins in state history.

"Maybe FOX News should start with the facts: the ACLU has repeatedly sued Kris Mayes over issues where they disagreed with her," Delaney Corcoran, the campaign manager for Mayes' re-election campaign, told Fox News Digital when asked about the email correspondence.

"Mayes has consistently fought for funding for Arizona police and cartel task forces — and stands shoulder to shoulder with Arizona sheriffs and police. Together, Mayes and law enforcement have seized 27 million fentanyl pills off of our streets, more than any other Attorney General in state history."

Mayes has defended Arizona against lawsuits from the ACLU challenging laws that allowed state and local police to arrest people illegally entering the country between ports of entry and restricted when people could film police officers. She later settled with the ACLU in the police filming case, agreeing to permanently prohibit the unconstitutional police recording law.

Though Mayes describes herself as a " moderate " and sparred with liberal legal groups, Barr — one of her top aides — repeatedly sought candidate recommendations from the progressive ACLU and PLO for corrections-related legal roles.
DRAG QUEENS, TRANS PASTOR, ABORTION RALLIES: INSIDE DEM GOVERNOR HOPEFUL'S PROGRESSIVE CHURCH

"I am looking to bring as much ADCRR work back in-house as possible in the Arizona AG’s Office. To do that, I need to hire attorneys to represent ADCRR in numerous capacities. If you know of anyone who may be interested in helping to turnaround things around here, please let me know," Barr wrote to representatives of the ACLU and PLO in February 2023.
In April of that year, Barr again turned to the groups, this time seeking possible candidates for ADCRR’s top legal position.

"Let me know if you have any suggested candidates," he wrote, forwarding an email to PLO and ACLU representatives soliciting applications for ADCRR general counsel. When his efforts to fill the role of ADCRR’s top lawyer bore no fruit, he again turned to the two groups.
"Still no takers for the ADCRR general counsel job. If you have any suggestions, please let me know," he wrote to them on May 11, 2023.
That same day, ACLU National Prison Project director David Fathi responded, promising to "redouble" his efforts to find a candidate for Barr.

Among the priorities of the ACLU National Prison Project are " substantially reducing the incarcerated population " and promoting a criminal justice system in which incarceration is used only as a " last resort ." Fathi has also criticized relying on police and prisons to address drug problems, stating in one social media post that "we will never solve drug problems with police and prisons."

Corene Kendrick, the deputy director of the National Prison Project, responded in turn to Barr's email that one of her possible recommendations was already "enjoying suing ADCRR in civil rights damages cases in her spare time of running her café in Carrizozo," showing that at least one prospective candidate being floated to Barr had experience suing ADCRR in civil-rights cases.
SOCIALISTS SET SIGHTS ON THE GROUND FLOOR OF GOVERNMENT AS GOP WARNS OF BIGGER PLAN UNFOLDING

Fox News Digital only obtained email records, not call transcripts or in-person meeting minutes, so it’s unclear what further assistance, if any, the PLO and ACLU gave the Arizona Attorney General’s Office. ADCRR ultimately hired Ashley Oddo to serve as its general counsel.

Before joining ADCRR, Oddo led Arizona State University’s Academy for Justice and had backed several criminal-justice positions associated with the left, including addressing systemic racism in policing and pardoning people convicted of nonviolent federal marijuana offenses.
Oddo has no institutional affiliation with the ACLU or the PLO nor was her name mentioned by either organization in email communications with Barr.

Other communications obtained and reviewed by Fox News Digital show a cordial relationship between Barr and staffers working for the ACLU and PLO. Fathi, for instance, requested a phone conversation with Barr in February 2023, and Barr responded two minutes later. Fathi disclosed in another email that the director of ADCRR reached out to him "to schedule a call about working together on ADCRR issues."
Don Specter, a longtime PLO attorney , also reported having a "productive meeting" with the head of ADCRR in June 2023.

To reduce incarceration, the PLO has pursued litigation that contributed to court-ordered reductions in California’s prison population, supported credit systems that can advance release or parole eligibility, and advocated reentry programs allowing eligible people to serve portions of their sentences in the community.
The organizations Barr turned to for recruiting assistance have taken positions on policing and incarceration that differ sharply from Mayes’ public law-and-order posture.
ARIZONA DEM AG BLASTED FOR 'DANGEROUS' CLAIM RESIDENTS CAN SHOOT ICE AGENTS UNDER STATE LAWS

"As Attorney General, Mayes has been a partner to law enforcement, delivering millions of dollars in funding and resources so border sheriffs and Arizona police can keep us safe," her campaign website reads. "She has locked up drug cartel members, seized more than 27 million deadly fentanyl pills off our streets and gone after criminals trying to take advantage of our kids."

The ACLU, meanwhile, has explicitly advocated defunding or divesting from police departments and redirecting resources toward other community services — publishing blogs with titles such as " Defunding the Police Will Actually Make Us Safer " and " Local Officials: Pledge to Divest from Police and Reinvest in Black Communities ." Additionally, the legal advocacy group has urged Congress to cut federal police funding while also calling on state and local leaders to reduce law enforcement spending .
The PLO likewise advocates reducing incarceration, expanding release opportunities and increasing community-based alternatives.
Those positions differ sharply from Mayes’ stated position on police funding. During her 2022 campaign, Mayes responded with " a resounding no " when asked whether she supported defunding the police.
Barr, Fathi, Oddo, Specter, Kendrick, the Arizona Attorney General’s Office, the ACLU and the PLO did not respond to requests for comment when reached by Fox News Digital on Monday.

articles.headline: Mercedes-AMG’s first ground-up SUV is a 1,150hp electric beast
keyFacts: Mercedes-AMG announced its first ground-up, full-size electric SUV, the 2028 AMG GT SUV, which delivers up to 1,153 horsepower.
The vehicle features an 800-volt architecture supporting charging speeds up to 710kW and is scheduled to launch in the US next summer.
Mercedes-AMG stated that pricing has not yet been officially released.
body: Earlier this year, Mercedes’ AMG performance brand grabbed our attention with the GT four-door coupe, a souped-up sports sedan with three axial flux motors delivering over 1,150 horsepower. Well, now meet its beefier cousin, the 2028 Mercedes-AMG GT SUV, an equally powerful, ultra-fast-charging electric people-hauler.
Mercedes-AMG’s first ground-up SUV is a 1,150hp electric beast
It may even out-muscle the Porsche Cayenne Turbo Electric and Lucid Gravity.

The AMG GT SUV (say that five times fast) marks the first time in the performance brand’s 59-year history that it has developed a full-size SUV entirely in-house from the ground up. Scheduled to hit the US next summer, the new EV is built on Merc’s high-performance AMG.EA architecture to combine sports-car handling with full-size SUV suburban practicality.

It will be available in three trims — GT 53, GT 55, and the flagship GT 63 — with the top model delivering 1,153hp via the same three axial flux motors powering the four-door coupe. That beats the Porsche Cayenne Turbo Electric with Launch Control, which is sure to make for some awkward run-ins around Stuttgart.

Thanks to an 800-volt architecture, the SUV supports blistering-fast charging speeds up to 710kW on the 128kWh battery (GT 63 / GT 55) and 600kW on the 106kWh battery (GT 53). Drivers can charge 10–80 percent in 12 minutes or gain up to 450km (around 280 miles) of WLTP range in just 10 minutes. The 128kWh battery trims will have an estimated max range of 435 miles.

That battery, by the way? It utilizes F1-inspired technology with specialized NCMA cathodes, silicon-containing anodes, and cylindrical cells. An electrically nonconductive oil flows directly around each individual cell for uniform thermal management, enabling continuous high-power delivery and long battery life. Mercedes has quietly been on the vanguard of battery technology for a while now, with the AMG GT SUV just the latest example. The 710kW charging speed, in particular, could give Mercedes another edge over Porsche’s 320kW speeds.

For a full-size SUV, the AMG GT sounds like it could handle like a vehicle half its size. Mercedes-AMG replaced the traditional mechanical roll bars with a newly developed suspension that uses active hydraulic elements to eliminate pitch and roll during acceleration, heavy braking, and cornering. Combined with three-stage air springs and standard six-degree active rear-axle steering, it purports to balance track precision with long-distance comfort.

But just because it’s a beefy lad doesn’t mean it’ll tip the scales. The AMG GT 63 SUV weighs in at 5,941lbs, making it slightly lighter than the Lotus Eletre R (6,007lbs) and Lucid Gravity (6,100lbs), and nearly identical to the Porsche Cayenne Turbo Electric (5,960lbs).

Silence is golden — except to a performance brand’s EV engineering team. That means piping in recorded sounds of real AMGs — in this case, the legendary AMG V8 and six-cylinder engines — to preserve the “emotional” AMG identity. Mercedes is proud that it’s using real engine sounds over synthetic EV tones, though some may disagree. The system even simulates mechanical gear shifts with paddle controls, offers adjustable sound profiles, and integrates physical seat vibrations — so you can still feel like there’s a real engine under that hood instead of a 78-liter frunk. The so-called AMGFORCE Sport+ drive program is offered as standard across all three trims of the Mercedes-AMG GT SUV.

Inside, you’ll find the MB.OS platform on your 14-inch display, with an army of AI agents from ChatGPT, Microsoft, and Google at your disposal to boss around. Use them to set navigation, discover random locations, do web searches, tell bad jokes, or whatever else people use AI for in their cars. Merc’s own onboard AI system can handle the physical stuff, like adjusting HVAC, changing drive modes, or fiddling with the lighting — all through voice commands.

Beyond voice and navigation, the AMG GT SUV applies AI to high-performance track driving through something called the Predictive Performance Manager. Mercedes says the PPM uses track-mapping data to dynamically throttle or boost electric motor output depending on topography, conserving battery energy on downhill or technical winding sections so full power is available on steep inclines and long straights. That could also mean faster, more consistent overall lap times by eliminating battery overheating and power throttling during track driving — something an AMG lover would likely appreciate.
Mercedes didn’t release the official pricing yet, though we can expect something closer to its official launch.
