articles.headline: No Publisher Wanted Outlast. 60 Million Players Later, The Horror Juggernaut Is Doing Just Fine.
keyFacts: Independent studio Red Barrels developed the 2013 horror game Outlast after failing to secure a publisher and funding from major companies like Ubisoft and EA.
Co-founder Philippe Morin said the team financed the game using $1 million from the Canada Media Fund, personal savings, and home mortgages.
Outlast achieved its first-year goal of selling 400,000 copies following promotional help, eventually expanding into a successful series.
body: Let's play Family Feud.

Poll 100 people on the scariest game they've ever played. What's on the board? Surely a Silent Hill, and a Resident Evil, too. Alien Isolation seems likely. One of the Fatal Frames has a good shot. Those who know ball may call out a deeper cut like Siren, Sylvio, or Visage. One name I'm certain makes it on the board--to the tune of my family cheering me on with "Good answer! Good answer!"--is Outlast .

The horror game from Montreal-based indie studio Red Barrels was released in 2013 as the debut effort from what was then a 10-person team. The studio was founded by developers with an origin story we hear about a lot in the games industry: They left roles at big-budget studios like Electronic Arts, Ubisoft, and Naughty Dog to pursue something they could call their own.

On an hour-long call with Red Barrels' Phillipe Morin, he told me how he and his co-founders, David Chateauneuf and Hugo Dallaire, established Red Barrels as a fully independent game studio and built what has become a tentpole horror series.
Content warning: This article contains descriptions of extreme violence.

"After our project got canceled at EA, we were having a hard time picking up on where we would want to go, what we would want to do," Morin said. "And so I think that's when we realized that we were pretty much all at the same place career-wise [and felt] it was time we try to make a project of our own."

Morin said the burgeoning team didn't know what its first game would be, but they landed on a horror game because that's what they were passionate about, with a distinct style to stand out: first-person, defenseless in nature--players could only run and hide from enemies, not fight back--with what would become the game's signature night-vision lens coloring the terror lurking around every corner.

"David was a huge horror fan, and I knew I would have a good time working on such a game. And Hugo came up with the idea behind the night vision and the visual style, mostly after watching the Rubber Johnny video."
The night-vision camera has become the signature trait of the Outlast series.

He explained that he and Chateauneuf tried to convince Ubisoft to let them make a horror game back in 2008 while they were still working there, but the developer-publisher wasn't interested, which Morin cited as "mostly a financial thing."

You might not remember, especially in today's much more horror-obsessed climate, but during that period--call it 2006 to 2012 or so--horror games had mostly gone dormant. There were a few exceptions, but most of them were moving the genre in an action direction, like Dead Space and Resident Evil 5, unless you were playing under-the-radar PC gems like Amnesia: The Dark Descent and Penumbra: Overture. Horror games weren't in , or so publishers that primarily dealt with AAA games believed, so they weren't looking to invest in them.

The co-founders figured Frictional Games' success with Amnesia proved there actually was a viable market for horror games, and they were grateful that the genre didn't become oversaturated in the first few years after Amnesia, leaving an opening for them. Morin recalled how quickly their expectations unraveled.
"We thought at first that we'd come up with the pitch within three or four months and shop it around to a few publishers, and we'd find out pretty quickly if it works or not," he said.
Instead, it took 18 months of meetings.

Partners were hard to come by; publishers were still obsessed with mobile games, a refrain I've heard often from developers who worked in that era. Morin remembered potential partners telling him that they'd "rather invest $50,000 in 10 mobile games than $500,000 in [Outlast]." Ultimately, the Canada Media Fund (CMF), a publicly funded investment program meant to support homegrown media projects across Canada, helped bring Outlast to fruition. But a million dollars from the CMF wouldn't be enough.
Morin told me the group put forward an additional $360,000 from their own savings accounts and credit cards, and leveraged their home mortgages to see the project through to the end.
"Everything was pretty much on the line," he reminisced. "Of course, it meant working very long, long hours. We were in a sprint to release the game before running out of money."
Morin remembered potential partners telling him that they'd "rather invest $50,000 in 10 mobile games than $500,000 in [Outlast]."

No publisher materialized, but the work continued, and eventually the team felt it could get the game to the finish line without an outside publisher, so Red Barrels did exactly that, though Morin admitted the team had no experience with that side of making video games.
"We were experienced game developers," Morin explained, "but we didn't know much about that side--publishing and marketing and sales and all that. So we had to learn on the fly."

A familiar name would come to Red Barrels' aid: Amnesia. Some folks at Red Barrels sat in on a conference talk by Frictional Games co-founder Thomas Grip, who said Frictional sold 400,000 copies of Amnesia: The Dark Descent in its first year on Steam. Red Barrels adopted that same total as its goal for Outlast, but after a promising launch window in early September 2013, sales slowed, suggesting they weren't on pace to hit it.
Morin reached out to Grip, who generously walked him through the ebb and flow of Steam sales.
"He explained to us the dynamic of Steam, and when you do promotion, it spikes back up, [then] goes back down, and basically your sales curve becomes like a roller coaster."
Outlast sought to stand on the shoulders of its similarly combat-free predecessor, Amnesia: The Dark Descent.
The game's first discount event, timed for Halloween that year, proved Grip correct, though Morin also recounted the boon of being featured on Conan O'Brien's Clueless Gamer segment .
"He played a bunch of horror games for Halloween, and his most positive comments were for Outlast, so that probably didn't hurt."

Five months after launching the game, Outlast had hit its year-one goal of 400,000 copies sold. They weren't all sold at full price, but it was enough for the whole team to enjoy "pretty significant bonuses," Morin said.

Around the same time, Outlast was ported to PlayStation 4 and included in its popular PlayStation Plus subscription at launch, which gave its brand another big boost. Without a gaming PC, and having eagerly awaited the game's console port after seeing it at Penny Arcade Expo in Boston a year earlier, I bought a PS4 just to play it myself. I joked with Morin that even though Sony didn't want to publish Outlast, he still made them at least a couple hundred bucks.

In the summer that followed, its Whistleblower DLC and subsequent Xbox launch kept it in the horror spotlight. It was still an era of few horror games, though there were signs of an upswing, with games like Alien Isolation, The Evil Within, and Hideo Kojima's PT--a free and immediately viral teaser for his eventually canceled Silent Hill project--all releasing before the year ended.

Even mobile games, once a roadblock for Outlast securing funding, were joining the horror trend, with Five Nights at Freddy's debuting that same year and becoming a streaming hit. Luckily for Red Barrels, Outlast had established what Morin called a "solid fanbase" by then, which the studio took as a sign that a sequel was in order.

But playing Outlast, or working on it, isn't for everyone. Not nearly. Even for players who consider themselves horror enthusiasts, the games are intense not only because players have no way to fight back against enemies, nor just because it's quite happy to leave you stranded in total darkness without any more camera batteries to power your light source, but also because of how far they go in their depictions of violence.
Along with the night-vision look, another aspect of Outlast helped it stand out: unflinching gore.

This is a series that asks its players to saw off the legs of a naked man hung on a crucifix; to inject a victim with a cocktail of STDs using a torture rack of syringes; to direct animatronics to drill into a man's penis and then decapitate him. Just typing out a few of the series' many nauseatingly graphic moments of unparalleled violence makes me a bit uncomfortable to admit I like these games.

Talking with Morin, I was finally able to ask something that was on my mind for years: Was Outlast, in its over-the-top depictions of violence, gore, and nudity--which, like horror itself, was much rarer in games back then--a reaction to the so-called "torture porn" trend in horror movies of the time, such as Saw, Martyrs, and Hostel? He told me it actually wasn't so calculated. Perhaps concerningly, it was simply a "personal preference."

"We didn't start like, 'Oh, we've got to make the goriest game out there.' It was just, 'We're making a horror game, so obviously we'll make it gory.' I remember even the scriptwriter early on was saying, 'There's never too much blood.'"

You can dig up some obscure titles on Steam or Itch.io that rival Outlast in how far a game pushes that proverbial envelope, but among mainstream successes, I haven't found anything that goes as far. I find it so far beyond the lengths other horror games go to that this relationship between tremendous success and unflinching gore is what inspired me to reach out to Red Barrels for this interview in the first place.

This degree of violence should mean Outlast is forever niche, or so I'd think, but it's been one of its biggest selling points, helping it become a household name among horror fans. Is that a sign of an increasingly depraved society? I don't think so. To me, it's just horror games catching up to horror movies in what people are willing to depict on screen.

"So we just started pushing and pushing and pushing, and you know, I remember there was a playtest, and somebody, after a couple of hours, basically ran out of the studio to go cry outside," Morin recalled, saying that she never came back. And she wasn't the only one.

"When we do job interviews, we always make sure that people are fully aware of the kind of content we create and the kind of conversations needed to create that content," Morin continued. "Again, people have to be comfortable with that because obviously you hear stuff in the studio that [if] you said the same thing in a different studio, you'd end up in a meeting with HR. We had one case of somebody who started working for us on Monday, and on Thursday they resigned because even though they knew about the gore and the violence, they had a blind spot for other things, more so about religion, and they were not comfortable with that, so they had to resign. So obviously it happens, but we try in our hiring process to make sure everybody knows what it takes to create these kinds of games."

Though the series has never shied away from incorporating religious iconography in its grisly scenes, Morin's anecdote most likely referred to Outlast 2, the 2017 sequel that again raised the profile of Red Barrels, which doubled in size to 20 people for the project. Like in the first game, players take on the role of a journalist following a tip that lands them in a nightmare. This time, it's a cult deep in the Arizona desert, telling a story inspired by the Jonestown Massacre.

Outlast 2 pushed the envelope so far that it actually had to scale it back a bit to avoid a ban in Australia for two scenes in particular. Later, when Red Barrels released a new difficulty in a patch, it re-added those scenes, though only to what is now considered the unrated PC version.

To date, very few games have ever scared me as much--I can count those that have on one hand, in fact. I told Morin that Outlast 2 was one of the hardest review assignments of my career, because I needed to finish before the embargo, but the game had tormented me. I often had to psyche myself up to play it.
This degree of violence should mean Outlast is forever niche, or so I'd think, but it's been one of its biggest selling points, helping it become a household name among horror fans.

Talking to him, I realized what I loved about Outlast 2 is what made it the most divisive game in the series. In Outlast, you're stuck in a cramped asylum, often with narrow corridors boxing you in. That can certainly be scary, and it was for me, too. But for Outlast 2, Red Barrels expanded its environments, often setting them outdoors in wide cornfields and other rural scenes. It sometimes made me less confident I was going the right way, which filled me with dread that I was needlessly spending extra time while a fanatic with a scythe hunted me, but Morin remarked that some players don't feel as stressed "if there is no roof."

Given how the team made ends meet without a publisher for the first game, by the time the second game was coming together, Red Barrels felt confident it could do it all alone again. And it did, but the game's launch wasn't as strong as the team had hoped. Morin said that was partly because of the physical edition of the series, Outlast Trinity, which bundled Outlast, its Whistleblower DLC, and Outlast 2 on disc.

"To this day, I'm still not sure [whether the physical edition] added sales, or did we just kind of cannibalize our digital sales and then get less money from it? Because obviously we get less money from a retail sale than digital," he said, adding that the Trinity edition was "too much stuff to handle" for Red Barrels at that time. It was another lesson one might learn when you're building a studio on the go.

Morin also found it frustrating because the first game shipped with an experience that was too easy, leading the team to add more difficulty options in post-launch patches to appease players who wanted a rougher go with it. But players said that Outlast 2 was too difficult at launch, which is a much harder fix. If a game is too hard, you lose the casual player base. They tend not to come back because they didn't care about the game as much as the hardcore fanbase--you've already scared them off. Meanwhile, players who want a greater challenge will more reliably return if a studio turns the dial that way, according to Morin.
Whereas Outlast touched on religion occasionally, Outlast 2 made it the focus.

"I make it sound like one was a success and the other one was a failure, which is not the case at all," Morin said. "Both games were pretty profitable, but it's just--I think at this point, we're able to acknowledge that there were a couple of things we could have done differently [with Outlast 2], and they would have affected the result in a significant way."

By the end of 2017, Red Barrels confirmed it wanted to do Outlast 3 eventually but noted that it had shifted focus to a new project. That would become Red Barrels' biggest project ever--in both scope and success: The Outlast Trials. Playable solo but intended as a co-op game for up to four players, The Outlast Trials was a reaction to the way many players were already playing Outlast, Morin explained.

"We knew that there were a lot of people playing the [earlier] games, but within a group. So people would watch it as they would watch a horror movie while somebody was playing, and then if that person died, then they'd give the controller to somebody else, and we were like, 'What if we can create that kind of experience, but everybody has a controller?'"

It would be six years between that seed of an idea and the early-access launch of The Outlast Trials in 2023, which Morin remembers as "a f**king long time" during which the team grew to 45 people and made "a shit-ton of prototypes." After four years, Red Barrels thought it had landed on something "shippable," Morin said, but a playtest went poorly and tanked enthusiasm.

The problem, he said, was the Red Barrels team "went too far trying to make [The Outlast Trials] systemic, random, and trying to reach our ultimate goal of infinite replayability. We needed to come back to something that maybe added less replayability, but definitely felt more like Outlast."

The team eventually found that formula and debuted it on Steam as an early-access game in 2023. In 2024, the 1.0 version arrived, along with its console release. Since then, it's received several major updates that have added features like a character prestige system, several more maps and abilities, an in-game shop, seasonal battle passes, and new villains, though none more memorable than the unnerving Mother Gooseberry who first greets players in the game's tutorial.
Critically and commercially, The Outlast Trials is among the most successful co-op horror games ever.

For the most part, I've felt Red Barrels has done a good job implementing live-service elements, even as the live-service landscape changed drastically between 2017 and 2024. However, some players have been disappointed with Red Barrels' use of generative AI for certain in-game elements, including posters players can unlock for their customizable Sleep Rooms, which they return to between rounds. I asked them about that, and they pointed me to their Steam disclosure regarding generative AI use.

As much as I enjoy Trials and still play it, I lost interest in completing its battle passes when I realized some rewards were made that way, though there are signs the team is in the process of replacing those assets with new ones that seem to be made by humans , even if it seems--to me anyway--the team doesn't want to celebrate that pivot for fear of creating a Streisand Effect -like reaction to the earlier use of those tools.

Early on, Morin explained, the team hadn't intended to create an Outlast live-service game. At first, they were focused on making an Outlast game people wanted to play with friends. Today, it's the best-selling and most-played Outlast game in the series, with nearly 19 million lifetime players, including those who jumped in during the game's stint as a PS Plus offering. Though the co-op nature of Trials gave the series a major overhaul, Morin said it's been a huge success because, at its heart, it's still Outlast.

"We've seen a lot of [live-service] games coming up, and they all try to beat Fortnite. They come up with all these different ways of getting revenue, but they don't focus enough on the main reason that people come back to your game in the first place: because the core loop is fun, and they enjoy the universe, and they want to spend more time in it. It's like opening up a restaurant and focusing too much on the wine selection--but the food has to be good first. Once you have people coming for the food, then you can maybe hope to sell them $200 bottles of wine."

Recently, The Outlast Trials quadrupled its personal-best Steam concurrent-player record , exceeding 120,000 players thanks to a hefty Steam discount, players' desire for scary games to play around Halloween , and a surge in China specifically. Outlast Trials' Season 7 is ongoing, with the annual Halloween event, Geister, set to begin before the month is through. Many live-service games seem intent on going forever, but that wasn't Red Barrels' original vision for Trials. I asked Morin if he now sees Outlast Trials as a forever kind of game.
"I think we're just scratching the surface. We'll stop making content when the players tell us to stop making content," he said.

Collectively, the Outlast series has attracted more than 60 million players. I asked the co-founder whether that type of success, with Trials in particular, makes getting back to Outlast 3 easier, because the team is buoyed by the live-service game, or more difficult, because it would draw resources away from what is already very successful to instead take a risk on what would presumably be another single-player game.

"Previously, we said that Outlast 3--we wanted to make it at some point. I don't think we've announced anything more official than that." Not wanting to overshare, he motioned to Red Barrels' marketing director, Marie-Joelle Paquin, who was listening in on the call. "I don't know, MJ, how far you want me to go."
"I think you've gone far enough for now," she replied. I couldn't help but laugh, having seen this kind of exchange so many times in this job.
Morin chuckled too, saying, "Sorry, Mark. I tried."
While players wait to learn more about Outlast 3, Trials continues to carry Red Barrels to new levels of success.

Fifteen years ago, Red Barrels couldn't find one company willing to publish Outlast. Today, the series is part of a distinct chapter in horror game history. Just as Silent Hill and Resident Evil inspired so many games that look and play like them, Outlast helped usher in a wave of horror games where players must run from relentless monsters, unable to fight back. Though Red Barrels doesn't claim to have invented this formula, it painted that burgeoning trend with its signature hues of blood-red gore and night-vision-tinted depravity.

There's renewed passion for horror, Morin said, even as so much else across the industry seems uncertain. The day before he and I spoke, another developer told him it seemed like the only studios in Montreal doing well were those making horror games: Red Barrels and Dead by Daylight's Behaviour Interactive. The genre's resurgence over the last several years has surely created more opportunities for studios to find publishers, opportunities that didn't exist when Outlast was incubating. But today, Morin is grateful things worked out the way they did because it's allowed Red Barrels to stay indie all this time.

"We've been working like this for 15 years. It would be hard to switch now," he told me, crediting the Outlast community for showing up in such huge numbers for the especially twisted horror series. "It's pretty funny and satisfying at the same time--that, considering the kind of content we put in our games, we've got such a nice bunch of people as a fanbase," even if, he joked, "some of them are maybe a little more f**ked up" than what Red Barrels has created.

articles.headline: Scuffles and fires break out as protesters rally across France, joining students
keyFacts: Police clashed with protesters who set fires across French cities during nationwide demonstrations, resulting in at least 272 arrests, authorities reported.
Demonstrators and students mobilized across France to protest rising living costs, including spiked gasoline, energy, and food prices.
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez suspended a type of police stun grenade after a 15-year-old lost a hand during protests.
body: Scuffles and fires break out as protesters rally across France, joining students

PARIS — A car and a newspaper kiosk were set on fire in Paris as police used tear gas and water cannons to disperse violent groups of protesters, while similar tensions erupted Saturday in other big cities on the fringes of nationwide demonstrations against rising living costs and in support of high school students' grievances.

Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez's office described "a growing number of violent incidents," including assaults on police officers, looting or attempted looting of shops and damage to public buildings. Authorities reported at least 272 arrests across the country, including in Paris.

In the French capital, police used tear gas and water cannons to push back people wearing hoods and masks and throwing fireworks and other objects at officers in the Place de la République, northeast of the Paris city center. Large numbers of riot police were deployed in the square and surrounding streets.

The majority of peaceful protesters joined a march that moved toward northwestern Paris. The crowd chanted France's national anthem as French flags were waved. The chants were accompanied by people playing trumpets and violins.
Meanwhile, police were working to prevent other small groups of protesters from converging on government buildings, Nuñez's office said.
Many metro stations were closed Saturday at police request, including those around the Champs-Elysées and near the presidential palace, parliament and government offices.
Violence hit Lyon, Marseille and other cities
In Lyon, France's third-largest city, where about 20,000 protesters joined the march, fire broke out inside a tourist office. Smoke and flames were seen rising from the building.
In the southern port city of Marseille, some shops and a municipal police station were damaged, while some protesters briefly forced their way into the lobby of City Hall.
"This is unacceptable," Marseille Mayor Benoît Payan told BFM TV, describing the damage in City Hall as "limited."
Nuñez's office also reported violence by masked groups in Rennes, Toulouse, Montpellier and Grenoble, among other cities.

Protesters across France responded to calls on social media to revive the "yellow vest" movement, which emerged in 2018 against social injustice. Demonstrators expressed widespread frustration and anger at the government as gasoline, energy and food prices have spiked in recent months.
Saturday's protests follow weeks of school blockades
Student groups protesting since mid-September through school blockades have urged supporters to join them.
The CGT, one of France's major labor unions, also backed the protests, calling for "higher wages and pensions, lower prices and the protection of public services that meet people's needs."

In recent weeks, France has seen thousands of arrests, hundreds of injuries and schools set on fire as the new school year descended into nationwide student protests that are influencing the country's presidential election campaign and drawing international attention.

Among protesters, particularly gruesome wounds suffered by some teenagers have been blamed on police riot-control weapons. Nuñez suspended the use of a type of police stun grenade against the young demonstrators after a 15-year-old lost a hand.
On Tuesday, climate and social justice activist Greta Thunberg joined students at a high school in the Paris suburb of Saint-Denis.

articles.headline: Ember’s new temperature-controlled mug makes my nightly tea ritual even better
keyFacts: Ember released the Mug 3 smart mug and the Tumbler 2, updating its temperature-controlled drinkware lineup.
The Mug 3 includes a physical temperature button, up to three hours of battery life, and top-rack dishwasher safety.
The Mug 3 is available on Ember's website, Target, and Amazon for $129 or $149 depending on size.
body: With the nights getting chillier, I’ve been reaching for a cup of tea more often. And if there’s one thing that can make a cozy fall night even better, it’s a warm drink that actually stays warm. Enter Ember’s new Mug 3, the latest version of the company’s temperature-controlled smart mug, which is designed to keep your drink at just the right temperature for as long as you sip.

Ember first introduced its smart mug in 2016 to solve a problem most coffee and tea drinkers know all too well: getting distracted for a few minutes, only to return to a lukewarm drink. Now, the company is back with its third-generation mug, which brings a handful of practical upgrades.

The biggest change is that you no longer have to open the app to adjust your drink’s temperature. Instead, you can use the button on the bottom of the mug to cycle through five preset temperatures, starting at 125 degrees Fahrenheit. Each press raises the temperature by five degrees, up to a maximum of 145 degrees, so you can easily make your drink a little hotter with each click.

Honestly, this is the feature I ended up using the most during my time testing out the mug. At night, when I’m curled up in bed with a book and a cup of tea, my phone is usually somewhere across the room. Being able to adjust my drink without getting up to find it is a small convenience, but one I genuinely appreciate.
It’s also a welcome change for users who have reported running into connectivity or pairing issues with the Ember app.

That said, I do have one complaint: the button is located on the bottom of the mug. It’s a peculiar design choice when you’re dealing with a cup full of hot liquid, and it isn’t particularly easy to press, either. I often found myself tilting the mug and pressing down firmly to get it to respond. So, while I appreciate the addition of on-mug controls, I wish Ember had made the button easier to reach.

If you prefer using your phone, the Ember app still offers plenty of customization. After pairing the mug with your phone over Bluetooth, you can choose presets based on what you’re drinking. Ember recommends 136 degrees Fahrenheit for black coffee, 132 degrees for green tea, and 142 degrees for lemon water. You can also create your own temperature presets, which is handy if you like your drinks a little hotter or cooler than the recommended settings.

The Mug 3 also comes with a few other upgrades, including a sliding lid designed to help prevent spills. The mug can also keep your drink at its desired temperature for up to three hours on a single charge. And it’s the first mug in Ember’s lineup to be top-rack dishwasher-safe, making cleanup easier. (Just keep in mind that it isn’t microwave-safe.)
The Ember Mug 3 comes in two sizes: a 10-ounce model for $129 and a 14-ounce version for $149.

The smaller mug is available in black, white, and stainless steel, while the larger size comes in eight colors, including sage green, lavender, powder blue, salt blue, sandstone, white, black, and matcha green.

Alongside the new mug, Ember also introduced the Tumbler 2, which replaces both the Travel Mug 2 and the original Tumbler in its lineup. The 16-ounce tumbler features a slimmer, taller design intended to fit standard car cup holders. It’s available in black for $179, while the Travel Mug 2 will remain available until supplies run out.
The products are available to purchase on Ember’s website, Target, and Amazon.

articles.headline: Trump traveling to Kentucky to rally supporters ahead of midterms
keyFacts: President Trump is traveling to Kentucky on Saturday to rally supporters and aid Republicans in competitive midterm races.
The visit matters because Republicans are defending narrow majorities in both the Senate and the House.
Kentucky Governor Andy Beshear said that Trump campaigning in the state suggests Republicans are in big trouble.
body: President Trump is heading to Kentucky Saturday to rally supporters and shore up Republicans facing unexpectedly competitive races — including a House contest that could put another seat at risk for the GOP.

Trump’s trip to Highland Heights, in Northern Kentucky, also puts him just across the Ohio River from battleground Ohio, where former US Sen. Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio) is trying to reclaim his seat from US Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio), who was appointed to fill the vacancy left by Vice President JD Vance.

Trump has visited Ohio four times during his current term, including two trips this month. During one visit, he joked about examining Husted’s backside — a reminder of the state’s importance as Republicans fight to preserve their 53-47 Senate majority and narrow 218-214 House majority.
The race is considered a pure tossup, in a state Trump carried against former Vice President Kamala Harris 55-44 in 2024, according to the Cook Political Report.
Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear, a potential 2028 presidential candidate, said Trump’s decision to campaign in a state he won handily was a troubling sign for Republicans.

“I don’t take any vote for granted” he told reporters this week. “But the fact that in the weeks leading up to this midterm election, the president’s coming to a state he won by 31 points that he believes he needs, suggest to me that Republicans are in big trouble,” he said, slightly padding Trump’s 30-point 2016 victory.

Trump’s rally also gives him access to Ohio television markets and a chance to demonstrate loyalty to a congressional candidate, Ed Gallrein, he helped push through a primary by opposing the incumbent, said University of Kentucky political scientist Stephen Voss.
It also puts Trump within reach of another congressional district where Republicans face a tougher fight, Voss said.
Rep. Andy Barr (R-Ky.) is hoping to fill Sen. Mitch McConnell’s (R-Ky.) seat, and is battling Democratic state Rep. Charles Booker.

A Global Strategy Group poll released by Booker’s campaign Sept. 9 had him trailing 49-40, with a margin of error of 4%. McConnell, 84, has occasionally bedeviled Trump, even while pushing through his court nominees and being sidelined by health challenges.

Barr’s Senate bid has opened up a House seat in the Lexington area, about a 90-minute drive from Trump’s rally. Democrat Zach Dembo, a former Navy JAG officer who left his job as a federal prosecutor in the Trump Justice Department, is challenging Republican Ralph Alvarado, a former state health commissioner.
The Cook Political Report moved the district Oct. 9 from “safe Republican” to the more competitive “leans Republican” category.

Republicans are favored in the state’s 4th Congressional District, where Trump helped knock off Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) in the primary, calling him a “nutjob”. Now, primary winner Ed Gallrein, a retired Navy SEAL, is taking on Democrat businesswoman Melissa Strange. Gallrein is favored, but some younger voters and indepdnents are threatening to stay home.
“Every once in a while you see a case where the electorate is angered so much that they sit on their hands,” said Voss.
Analysts say persistent inflation, the Iran war, and fuel costs have made races competitive across the country even in Republican-leaning territory.
Trump’s trip followed visits to Alaska, Montana, and Georgia this week.

articles.headline: Elon Musk agrees to settle lawsuits over 2024 election lottery
keyFacts: Elon Musk and America PAC agreed to settle two lawsuits alleging they defrauded voters with a daily million-dollar giveaway before the 2024 election.
Arizona plaintiffs claimed Musk and America PAC misled voters in seven swing states into signing a petition supporting the US Constitution.
The settlements are subject to court approval, and the court filings did not include the settlement terms.
body: Elon Musk and his America Pac political action committee said recently that they agreed to settle two proposed class actions alleging the billionaire entrepreneur defrauded residents in closely contested states before the 2024 US election by promising voters a lottery-style daily $1m giveaway.
The plaintiffs, Musk and America Pac told the judge overseeing the two related lawsuits in federal court in Austin, Texas, on Thursday that they have reached settlements subject to court approval.
The filings did not include settlement terms, and lawyers involved in the case declined to comment or did not respond to requests for more information.

The plaintiffs in the two cases are Arizona residents who said Musk and America Pac misled voters in seven swing states into signing his petition to support the US constitution by promising $1m daily to randomly selected signatories.
The defendants denied the allegations.
Musk founded America Pac to support Donald Trump as he successfully ran in November 2024 for a second US presidency.
A federal judge in June said Musk – the CEO of Tesla and SpaceX as well as the owner of the social media platform X – must testify in the lawsuits.

articles.headline: Plug-in solar is legal in these 10 states now – how it could save you money
keyFacts: Ten states, beginning with Utah, have legalized backyard and plug-in solar systems for residential use.
Plug-in solar lowers electric bills, but utility opposition and home wiring concerns keep it illegal in many states.
About two dozen states are considering legalization bills, with some advancing and others stalled until the 2027 legislative session.
body: ZDNET’s key takeaways
- Multiple states are working to legalize backyard solar setups.
- After Utah, nine other states have legalized it, or are working on bills for plug-in solar.
- 24 other states are stalled but already working on legislation.

Plug-in solar systems are easy to set up and can save consumers money on their power bills, but they’re still illegal in many states. Utah was the first to legalize backyard and plug-in solar, but other states have since caught on, and more are working on their own pathway to legalization.

As we’ve covered before, these plug-in solar setups (also commonly called “backyard solar”) are plug-and-play systems consisting of one or more solar panels, an inverter, and a battery. The system connects to a home’s standard 120-volt outlet, automatically routing solar-generated electricity from the battery to the nearest running appliance.
More from ZDNET
What states have legalized plug-in solar?

Ten states have already legalized backyard and plug-in solar systems, so residents there can already purchase and install systems like the EcoFlow Stream in their homes. Here’s the current status of the states that have already successfully passed legislation, legalizing such devices for consumer use.
Data sourced from Solar.com.
What states are working to legalize plug-in solar?

About two dozen states are still in the process of legalizing plug-in solar. Some bills have stalled until the next legislative session reconvenes in 2027, while others are going through committee hearings.

Balcony solar bills H.5175 and S3143 are advancing in Massachusetts, and the SUNNY Act is pending governor approval in New York. Bills in other states like Michigan, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, South Carolina, and Washington, DC have reached committee hearings.

Most states have stalled plug-in solar bills until the next legislative session in 2027, including Alaska, Arizona, Delaware, Hawaii, Idaho, Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Minnesota, Missouri, North Carolina, and Oklahoma.

Unfortunately, plug-in solar bills have failed in Georgia, New Mexico, Oregon, Washington, and Wyoming, so if you live in one of those states, these kinds of devices are technically illegal to operate. This doesn’t mean that it won’t eventually clear the legislative slate in these states, but lawmakers will need to file a new bill to reintroduce them after making necessary revisions.
Can I set up my solar panels if my state legalizes plug-in solar?
Whether you can immediately set up your balcony solar panels or not after the systems are legalized in your state will depend on your home situation.

Generally speaking, the bills in question focus on preventing utility companies from blocking plug-in solar projects. These bills can’t preempt bans on these systems by landlords or HOAs, though supplementary bills have been introduced in some states to include protections for HOAs and landlords.
Why is plug-in solar illegal?

Plug-in solar is illegal because the electrical systems in traditional American homes aren’t designed to receive power from a standard wall outlet. Rooftop solar systems are professionally installed and designed so the energy harvested by the panels flows through a circuit breaker and into your outlets. Plug-in solar, in turn, introduces electricity directly into an outlet, bypassing the electrical panel.

In a plug-in solar setup, nearby appliances draw energy supplied by the breaker and the solar inverter, but the wiring could carry more current than the breaker alone would allow before it trips. But it’s not solely about safety.

Installing your own solar panels means less reliance on local utilities. These companies are the biggest regulatory obstacle for plug-in or balcony solar setups. Their rules and regulations on solar energy are designed for rooftop panels, not plug-and-play systems, so legislation should push utility companies to change that.

There’s also the elephant in the room: utilities would make less money off their services if plug-in solar becomes widely popular. When consumers purchase less electricity, they contribute less to grid costs.

articles.headline: Republicans have a huge fundraising advantage. Will it matter?
keyFacts: Republicans have built a large fundraising advantage over Democrats ahead of the midterm elections, New York Times reporter Shane Goldmacher said.
Republican campaign cash could limit Democratic seat gains despite polls predicting a midterm blue wave, Goldmacher stated.
Republicans are spending heavily on advertisements to defend Senate seats in Texas, South Carolina, and Kansas, Goldmacher reported.
body: “Wwhen you talk about how many seats can the Democrats gain, given how unpopular Trump is, the Republican money is seen as a real limiter on Democratic chances,” New York Times reporter Shane Goldmacher told Vox’s America, Actually podcast. | Alex Wong/Getty Images

Polls and pundits alike are widely — if sometimes cautiously — predicting a blue wave in the midterm elections on November 3. But there’s an important caveat to predictions of a Democratic triumph: Republicans have far more cash at their disposal.

President Donald Trump’s super PAC alone had around $400 million on hand earlier this fall, and Elon Musk has personally pumped hundreds of millions into critical races, including $158 million for Texas alone .

Democrats, by contrast, have lagged far behind, especially relative to their performance in past cycles, with the party’s candidates propped up more by small-money donors than deep-pocketed institutional players.

Shane Goldmacher, a national political reporter for the New York Times, has extensively covered the role of money in American electoral politics. He spoke with America, Actually host Astead Herndon about where that money is coming from, how the GOP is spending it, and the effect that it might have on the coming elections.
They also discuss the races that aren’t getting funded — and what current fundraising patterns might tell us about the candidates who could be in the mix in the next presidential campaign cycle.

Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full show, so listen to America, Actually wherever you get your podcasts or watch it on Vox’s YouTube channel .

A couple of weeks ago we asked, “What is the GOP strategy to try to win?” And one of the answers we got is they simply have more dollars than Democrats. Everyone’s talking about this GOP money advantage, but how big is it really, and where is it coming from?

It’s bigger than I’ve basically seen in the last 20 years, and it’s almost entirely coming from big donors. President Trump has a super PAC. It had about $400 million in it at the beginning of September, and there was no Democratic counterpart.

And then the Republican National Committee, which is functionally controlled by Trump, had another $130 million . More than Democrats, because the DNC has literally more debts than cash . That’s a half a billion dollars.
You’re saying this is a historic edge.

In 2024, Kamala Harris outspent Donald Trump significantly in the general election. In 2020, Joe Biden significantly outspent Donald Trump in the general. In 2016, Hillary Clinton . And in the midterms along the way, same story .
This is a switch, and when you talk about how many seats can the Democrats gain, given how unpopular Trump is, the Republican money is seen as a real limiter on Democratic chances.
Do we know anything specific about the people putting in money to the Trump super PAC and the RNC to give them such a lead?

Most of these folks are disclosed. And Trump has been pretty open about raising money from the very moment that he won. He’s been pretty clear that he is in business to help people who are helping him. And so there are big crypto industries that are giving money that are expecting or hoping for favorable regulation from the administration.
So it’s a lot of big businesses. It’s a lot of wealthy Republicans who generally support him anyway, and there are industry groups that see benefit to being in favor.

I will never forget, obviously, the scene from Trump’s second inauguration when he had the Zuckerbergs and the Bezoses and Elon Musk behind him . Is that how I should think about the people funding this donor advantage? Is it tech oligarchs? Is it tech forward?

There’s a lot of tech. I wouldn’t say it’s exclusively [tech]. And Musk, by the way, is like an extra pot of money. Musk, the world’s richest person, is said to be spending at least $200 million . So that’s a bigger chunk. He has given some money directly to the Trump super PAC . He’s given some money to these congressional super PACs .

Is this just quid pro quo? Is this just a group of businesses who think, “Hey, no matter how unpopular this guy is, it is worth investing in him and his party because they’re gonna, regulate or not regulate in a way that’s favorable for us”?
It’s not quite just that. He raised a ton of this money when he was not so unpopular. If you want to say something smart that he did, it was that. Throughout 2025 he was raising all of this money.
And I don’t want to overstate the Republican advantage. A lot of these Democratic candidates are raising a ton of money. James Talarico stands out as maybe the peak example of this.

The Texas Senate race is the most expensive race in the country right now , and Republicans are pouring $200 million to save the nominee there. So a big chunk of that advantage is going to Texas. And the Democrats have put very little money from outside groups into Texas .

Talarico has captured the imagination of these small Democratic donors, and he’s raised tens and tens of millions of dollars . I would be shocked if he doesn’t hit $100 million by the end of the cycle.
You reported that the GOP’s pulling back in North Carolina. What should we take from that in terms of how the GOP sees its own landscape when it comes to the federal races?

Where have Republicans put that money? They put it into South Carolina right next door to protect a seat that was once thought, on the Senate front, to be safe for Republicans. This is the former Lindsey Graham seat that his sister is now running in . And then even more of it has gone to Kansas. This is a state that has not elected a [Democrat] to the Senate for nearly 100 years .

If you’re the Republican Party and you’re pulling money out of a state like North Carolina that hasn’t elected a Democrat since 2008 , and then putting it into a place that hasn’t elected one since 1932, that tells you where the, the bar is moving.
I think the concern for Democrats right now is there might be a wave, but Kansas has a big red wall. It’s hard to beat that kind of institutional advantage for the Republican Party.
Considering how close we are to Election Day, like, what are they actually spending this money on? Is it just more ads? Is it just more mailers?

I was in Pennsylvania this month, and I was trying to watch political ads on YouTube for various races. And I was getting pre-roll of three political ads before I watched the political ad I was trying to watch. So much about our elections is being decided now by people who are actively trying not to consume political news. It costs more money to reach people who are avoiding it on purpose.
There are some organizing things that happen, but most of the money is various versions of advertising.
On the Democratic side, considering this GOP edge, what are the races that you currently describe as underfunded? Where do the Democrats wish they had more money?
Number one is governors’ races, actually. When you look at where Democratic donors swoon, it’s Senate races. There are no candidates for governor who have made people swoon like this in recent years.

[James] Talarico is raising all this money, but in Texas also, Gina Hinojosa, the Democratic candidate for governor, does not have that kind of money, and she’s running against Greg Abbott, who had $100 million .
What should we ascribe that to?

I think there’s actually a pretty simple answer, which is, if you don’t live in the state, it doesn’t impact you. If you’re a small donor and you live in California, you can be excited about a Senate candidate because you want Democrats to control the Senate. Are you as excited about a Democratic governor of Georgia?
It’s hard to argue that the governors of these key presidential battlegrounds aren’t some of the most important races on the ballot this year.

By the way, a problem with both parties. Republican national donors and these super PACs also don’t fund these governor’s races at the same level. So it’s not just a Democratic issue, but it’s more acute [for them] because Democrats are so well-funded at the small-donor level.

Fundraising is a huge part of what sets the presidential candidates apart from one another. The money game among those candidates has already started. Is there anyone who’s quietly built some donor network that’s worth thinking about? Is there someone who stood out as a particularly effective fundraiser when we think about the 2028 crowd?

Let me give you my favorite stat from the last Democratic primary, which is that Mike Bloomberg spent twice as much as Tom Steyer, who spent twice as much as Bernie Sanders, who spent twice as much as Joe Biden, who became the Democratic nominee. And so money isn’t gonna determine who wins the next Democratic presidential primary.

One person who has unlimited money, functionally, is JB Pritzker. He’s a billionaire, the governor of Illinois, and he is spending his money now to help other Democrats , which is a good way to make friends.
My last question is an open one. What’s an underexplored story that we should be following going forward when it comes to campaign cash or both parties’ relationship with money?

One of my big questions is what happens to Republican small-dollar fundraising in that post-Trump era. Because there have basically not been any other Republicans who have excited donors for a decade.
Not JD Vance?

I have not seen evidence. JD Vance was not a good fundraiser before he [joined] the ticket with Donald Trump. When he ran for Senate, his primary run was funded chiefly by Peter Thiel through a super PAC.

There are candidates who’ve raised some money, but nothing on the scale of what these Democratic candidates have been able to raise online. When you talk about that Trump era [ending] at some point, are there others who are going to get Republican small donors excited? We don’t know. We haven’t seen it yet.

articles.headline: Yes, You’re Probably Paying More for Phone Service. Here’s Where Your Money Is Going
keyFacts: T-Mobile, AT&T, and Verizon have raised fees and legacy plan prices, increasing overall costs for mobile phone customers.
These fee hikes bypass multi-year price guarantees because those protections apply only to base plans rather than added fees.
Customers can lower their monthly expenses by switching to prepaid carriers, downgrading service tiers, or utilizing free network trials.
body: Everything is getting more expensive bit by bit, and it’s not just gas or grocery prices. T-Mobile just increased the price of a pair of fees that get added on top of what customers pay for their mobile phone plans, and it’s not the only carrier doing this.
Over the past year and a half, the big three US cellular providers have raised prices in small ways that may not seem consequential month to month, but add up over the year.
More costly fees, taxes and plans

For a while, a lot of carriers’ plans rolled taxes and fees into them as a competitive advantage — when you know you’re paying a fixed amount each month, it’s easier to budget. Unfortunately, those days are over, at least among the big three US carriers: AT&T, T-Mobile and Verizon.
More from CNET

The new fee increases are so small that you probably won’t notice them on your bill. Effective Oct. 12, T-Mobile’s Regulatory Programs and Telco Recovery fees increased for every line on a customer’s account. For voice lines, it’s an increase of $1.00 for the combined fees (previously $4.49 a month, now $5.49 a month). Mobile internet lines, such as those for smartwatches or tablets, went up $0.50, from $2.10 to $2.60 a month.

T-Mobile previously raised the cost of these fees in April 2025, from $3.49 to $3.99 and $1.40 to $1.60, so in a year and a half, customers are paying $2 more per voice line and $1 more per mobile internet line per month.

Even if your plan has a multi-year price guarantee, that applies to the main plan itself, not miscellaneous taxes and fees that are added on top of the plan’s cost. Carriers can, and do, increase those fairly regularly.
For Roger Entner, analyst and founder of Recon Analytics, the problem isn’t that carriers regularly raise fees like this. It’s that they spread out the increases.

“I don’t understand why they [don’t] only piss you off once a year, but instead sometimes choose to piss you off four times a year,” Entner said in a conversation with CNET. “It doesn’t make sense unless you want to be hated.”

T-Mobile isn’t the only one that’s increased these fees. AT&T raised its Administrative and Regulatory Cost Recovery Fee from $3.99 to $4.99 per line in August; that was after a December 2025 increase from $3.49. Verizon raised its fees in August 2025, from $3.50 to $3.78 per month for voice lines and from $1.60 to $3.97 per month for data-only lines.

As for the prices of the plans themselves, they’ve been relatively consistent. The exception is Verizon, which announced holiday deals in December 2025 and carried the pricing all the way through August when it announced the Simplicity plan. The myPlan plans, which include Unlimited Welcome, Unlimited Plus and Unlimited Ultimate, now cost $10 more per line for new customers than they did at the beginning of 2026.

Are these costs enough to inspire customers to look elsewhere? “We’ve done research on what makes people [switch carriers],” Entner said. “Five dollars and below doesn’t matter. People shrug it off. … Where the outrage [would be] is if your price would go up by $15, $20, and nobody’s doing that.”
Retiring legacy plans

When AT&T revamped its unlimited phone plan lineup in March this year. It also announced that prices would be increasing for many of its “retired” plans, as much as $20 for an account (not per line). Then, in August, the increases were applied to more legacy plans, which included the ones that the new 2.0 plans had just replaced a few months earlier.

At the time, an AT&T spokesperson said, “This increase reflects the real cost of continuing to deliver the speed, reliability and support our customers expect every day.” I think it’s also safe to say that this type of increase can also serve as an incentive for customers to migrate to current plans.

In June, however, T-Mobile announced it would unilaterally move some customers to new plans in order to get their old ones off the books. Although T-Mobile said that most plans would be comparably priced to what the customers were paying before, in some cases it meant increases of up to $6 per line per month.
The new plans were variations of T-Mobile’s existing lineup, such as Experience More with Appreciation Savings versus the straight-up increase that switching to the Experience More plan entails.
The move wasn’t optional, and at least one customer filed an informal complaint with the FCC. That’s one step below a formal complaint, which would involve fees and lawyers.
Price guarantees have almost evaporated

In April of last year, Verizon made a big deal about offering a three-year price guarantee on all of its plans. However, the guarantee slipped away in August when the company introduced its Simplicity plan. T-Mobile one-upped Verizon with a five-year price guarantee on its plans, which is now available only on the Experience Beyond 2.0 and Experience More 2.0 plans.
The people who signed up for plans under those terms still enjoy the price protection, but customers looking to jump to a new carrier won’t necessarily get the same deal now.
For existing customers, price guarantees can also act like handcuffs. If they want to move to another Verizon plan, for example, they’ll have to give up that price stability.
Looking at the bigger picture, though, wireless service has gotten cheaper

When I was researching for this article, I came across one written by Entner for LightReading that takes a longer-term view of wireless pricing. It highlights that we’re actually paying less for phone service now than we used to. In “Inflation mostly skipped the wireless bill,” Entner uses industry and government data to show that wireless service has gotten cheaper in real terms since 2007 (the year the iPhone was released).

“The dollars that you spend, yes, it’s going up,” Entner said in our conversation. “When we calculate it as part of your wallet share, [the] percentage of your monthly disposable income, it goes down.”
How can you save money on your phone bill?

A couple bucks in fees here and there doesn’t sound like a lot, but if you have four lines on an account, for example, that’s an extra $8 per month you weren’t paying before. And for people looking for the most economical plan, it’s a larger percentage of their phone bills.
So what options are there to offset the increases or reduce your monthly expense?

One option is to shop around for a prepaid plan. Companies such as Cricket, Mint Mobile and Visible run on the carrier’s networks and can cost less, especially if you’re currently paying for perks such as streaming services or hotspot data you’re not using. (Those three are all actually owned by the big three: Cricket is AT&T, Mint Mobile is T-Mobile and Visible is Verizon). Another option is US Mobile, which lets you choose whichever network is strongest in your area.

A single line on T-Mobile’s Essential Saver 2.0 plan, for example, costs $50 and includes 50GB of high-speed data. Mint Mobile’s 12-month Unlimited plan works out to $30 a month when you prepay $360 for the entire term, and it also includes high-speed data that may be slowed after you use 50GB. It includes up to 20GB of mobile hotspot usage, too.
Although it’s a bigger one-time lift, prepaying for an entire year for a plan like this means you won’t have to wonder how much next month’s bill will be.
You may not be in a position to switch providers, particularly if you’ve financed a phone from your current carrier. But you may be able to drop back to a less expensive plan with fewer features.

Verizon’s Simplicity plan at $45 a month, for example, is $20 less expensive than its Unlimited Welcome myPlan for a single line. (Verizon touts the $30 a month price, but that’s just for new customers who bring their own phone with them.) And Simplicity actually gives you better performance, because you can connect using the faster 5G Ultra Wideband (or 5GUW) if your phone has the hardware for it; Unlimited Welcome is limited to regular 5G speeds.

But Simplicity has an important catch: If you have a multi-line Verizon plan and one person switches to Simplicity, every other line must also switch to it. For a family of four, that means paying $180 a month (at the $45 rate), which is $10 more expensive than the Unlimited Plus myPlan and includes less high-speed mobile hotspot data.

As another example, AT&T’s modular Build-A-Plan costs as little as $15 a month when you bring your own unlocked AT&T-compatible and eSIM-capable phone. That gives you just 1GB of data — and that’s it, but you can add more data and hotspot capability for additional costs.

Then there’s the free option. If you don’t mind ads and the restriction of using a single app for all your communications, TextNow gives you calling, texting and data for email, maps, ride-sharing and finance apps. Unlimited data and calling plans can be purchased for the day ($3), week ($9) or month ($36).

If you’re thinking of switching providers, don’t forget that each one has limited programs to let you test out the speed and coverage in your area. T-Mobile offers a free three-month Network Pass, Verizon has a 30-day “trial” program and AT&T has its own 30-day eSIM free trial program.

It’s never fun to find the bill for your wireless phone service — an expense that feels like a modern necessity — is going up. But there are plenty of alternative options that can save you money, if you know where to look.

articles.headline: Cybercrims go beyond stealing data to attack physical building systems
keyFacts: Cybercriminals hacked remote-controlled refrigeration systems across hundreds of French grocery stores, spiking temperatures, spoiling food, and sparking fires.
Armis Labs reported that ransomware attackers increasingly use physical disruptions from compromised building automation systems as extortion leverage.
Security experts stated that attackers will increasingly target internet-connected operational technology as organizations improve their information technology defenses.
body: Late Sunday night, a still-unknown cybercriminal or group hacked thousands of remote-controlled refrigeration systems across hundreds of French grocery stores, spiking temperatures, spoiling food, and sparking fires. This is part of an ongoing trend of attacking physical systems that can do damage in the real world.
In August, a ransomware attack disrupted building-management systems at a Canadian hospital, affecting door access controls, central HVAC monitoring, and the issuing of staff access cards.

And three years ago, cyberattacks hit Las Vegas casinos, causing slot machines to go dark, preventing payment kiosks and ATMs from spitting out cash, and locking guests out of their rooms when the electronic keys stopped working.

Not all digital intrusions remain in cyberspace, and attackers don’t need to encrypt files and steal data to cause chaos. Hitting physical systems often produces more severe consequences - and turns up the heat on executives to pay an extortion demand.

“There was one gig where the customer was refusing to pay, and so the threat actor was like, ‘Hold my beer, have fun getting into your offices,’ and locked everybody out,” Tim Beasley, a senior incident response consultant at Semperis, told The Register.
Beasley won’t name the customer, or provide any incriminating information, but said the incident response involved police smashing glass in addition to his team recovering compromised data.

“The cops had to break in, and literally get into the building, breaking some windows, so the customer was able to finally get back in,” he said. We asked if the customer paid the ransom demand, and Beasley yelled: “Oh, hell, no!”

A report published earlier this month by ServiceNow’s Armis Labs found increasing evidence of ransomware attackers using physical consequences as leverage in their intrusions. “Today’s BAS operate at the intersection of IT and OT worlds, creating unprecedented exposure,” the report said.
Ransomware with physical consequences

Building automation systems - BAS - are the critical systems that control and monitor facilities’ HVAC, lighting, energy usage, and water consumption. They also oversee badge readers, door locks, surveillance cameras, fire alarm control panels, and other physical safety equipment.

As such, BAS make very attractive targets for ransomware operators looking for high-pressure ways to extort organizations into paying multi-million ransom demands. These systems also appeal to government-backed goons and hacktivists looking to ensure maximum psychological and physical impact during destructive cyberattacks.

Armis Labs found 73 percent of organizations own BAS that have been used in ransomware attacks, and this same percentage have known exploited vulnerabilities in at least one of their building automation systems. Additionally, 91 percent of BAS communicate over insecure protocols - opening up an even bigger attack surface for cyber-miscreants wanting to cause physical harm.

“The primary thing that we see with any attack on building management systems or physical systems: It’s a great place for the threat actor to hide,” Michael Freeman, ServiceNow’s senior director of threat research, told The Register. “It's easier for them to compromise, and it's easier for them to hide in.”

BAS and operational technology (OT) in general have fewer security controls than IT systems. Most require continual uptime, which makes them harder to patch or even scan for vulnerabilities and misconfigurations as this may lead to outages.

“One case in particular, against a very large financial institution, the threat actors were staying low and quiet by attacking their BMS systems, and then pivoting into the IT environment,” Freeman said.
The intruders were routinely caught - and booted from - the financial institution’s IT systems, so they built backdoors into the BMS to ensure persistent access to both OT and IT networks.
“We're also seeing threat actors using AI to understand more building automation systems, especially ones that are using obscure OSs like VxWorks, older Unix-type systems,” Freeman said.
AI has entered the chat

As multiple security experts have told us in previous interviews, security through obscurity is dead. Not only does AI make it easier for attackers to find bugs – some very obscure and decades old - but it also means criminals no longer need to be OT experts to carry out destructive cyberattacks on critical networks and facilities. Instead, they can use AI to learn all about the obscure protocols and proprietary hardware and software that historically made industrial control systems black boxes.
“It’s easier to understand what the controls are,” Freeman said, using the example of an attacker trying to take down a plane, or some similar catastrophic cyberattack.

Historically, even advanced, government-backed hacking squads would “be quiet, because you don't know what changing certain settings is going to do,” Freeman explained. “Now you can use AI to say, ‘If I compromise a weight and balance system for airlines, all I need to do now is move this number here to this number, and I just told the system to load heavy stuff on the right side of the plane instead of equal distribution.'”

Freeman told us he has seen attackers break into airlines’ OT gear in the past. “But they didn’t know what they were getting into, and so they left them alone,” he said. “Those do cause me concern because in the past I've helped to kick people out of those types of systems.”
Industrial orgs increasingly under attack

OT security provider Dragos tracks ransomware groups’ claims against industrial organizations on the criminals’ leak sites, along with publicly disclosed intrusions affecting manufacturing and other critical sectors. To be clear: claims on leak sites aren’t always accurate or even true, and the claim itself doesn’t mean operations or control systems were hit.
Since 2022, however, “the numbers have been consistently increasing,” Lexie Mooney, senior threat analyst at Dragos, told The Register.
The cybersecurity firm tracked 995 ransomware attacks against industrial orgs in 2023, a 49.5 percent increase from 2022. That number jumped more than 87 percent in 2024.
Active ransomware groups targeting industrial orgs also grew in 2024 to 80 groups, up from 50 the year before.

Dragos tracked 119 ransomware groups impacting more than 3,300 industrial organizations in 2025, and the incidents have steadily increased every quarter this year: 1,020 incidents in the first quarter of 2026 and 1,140 incidents in Q2.

“The vast majority of cases are opportunistic,” Abdul Alamri, a senior threat analyst at Dragos, told us. “In some of the cases that we have seen an operational impact, either physical systems or an OT operation, it’s just the nature of the opportunism on the part of those ransomware groups.”

This is partially due to the complexity of OT systems, he added. “Ransomware groups want to disrupt operations, and put pressure on the victims to pay the ransom,” Alamri said. “They don’t want to invest that time and effort to target complex systems."

It’s usually quicker and easier for financially motivated crims to affect operations via IT systems - as the extortionists did in the August 2025 Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) breach, which halted manufacturing and crippled business operations for months.
Internet-connected OT: the next 'low-hanging fruit'
The other side of this complexity, however, is that many organizations themselves still lack visibility into their OT environments.

Dragos estimates that fewer than 10 percent of OT networks worldwide currently have sufficient network monitoring in place. Plus, in 30 percent of incidents the security firm responded to in 2025, the investigations did not begin with a detection alert, but with someone noticing that “something seemed wrong” in operations.

This lack of visibility, combined with threats from AI, worries Alamri. “If you compare the risk that we have seen from humans, to what we are about to face in the near future with AI agents who might continuously try to break into those systems - it’s a pretty dark future if we don't take the right measures to protect ourselves against it.”

As organizations get better at patching and securing IT systems, attackers will likely look to internet-connected OT systems where digital compromises have real-world consequences, according to Matt Hayden, VP of cyber and emerging threats at General Dynamics Information Technology.
“We all anticipate that as we get better at reducing the IT low-hanging fruit, OT will become a vector of much more scrutiny and much more attention,” Hayden told The Register.
Before joining GDIT, Hayden served as the assistant secretary for cyber, infrastructure, risk and resilience policy at the US Department of Homeland Security.
Compliance vs. security

“There is a big focus on the hardware being connected for the purpose of compliance - and to make sure that, in the name of compliance, we aren't opening back doors, to devices that traditionally wouldn't have to be connected to facilitate their service,” he said, using refrigeration units as an example of one such system that is now internet-connected for compliance purposes.
This was prior to the French supermarket hacks.

Refrigeration units’ monitoring systems connect to the internet so their owners and operators can prove to regulators that the units maintain their uptime and temperature in accordance with regulations.

“So if the health department comes by, they say, ‘Look, my refrigerator was at 27 degrees for the last 72 days,' and they have a check mark, and they get their A plus. But that simple connectivity is also a vector in which that particular refrigerant unit could be targeted for disruption,” Hayden said.
About a week after our interview, criminals did exactly that.

“The recently reported exploitations of commercial refrigeration units represent a significant example of devices without digital value, no sensitive data or extended enterprise access, being exploited by being connected to the internet with unpatched firmware,” Hayden told us in a subsequent email.
He said he expects the attribution to be “less nation-state, and more likely those looking for targets of opportunity to identify what could be done with the unpatched systems.”
“The consequences are food supply degradation at a small scale, but it is an important example of what could happen at scale very quickly with more consequential operating equipment,” Hayden said.®

articles.headline: Science says your boss should talk less in meetings
keyFacts: Close to one billion meetings take place globally each day, occupying nearly three-quarters of CEOs' workdays.
Meeting science is expanding rapidly among psychologists due to large amounts of data from archived virtual meetings.
Psychologist Liana Kreamer coauthored a review spanning three decades of meeting science to study workplace behavior.
body: Close to 1 billion meetings take place each day around the world. CEOs spend nearly three-quarters of their workdays in meetings. Planning for and spearheading meetings eats up the lion’s share of managers’ time. In much of the industrialized world, meetings are both the metronomes and menaces of people’s working lives.

Given the enormous time spent in workplace meetings, do we know what they accomplish or how to make them as worthwhile as possible? For decades, the answer was… not really. Meetings weren’t a particularly accessible subject of study. But that has changed. Once a tiny niche area, “meeting science” is a growing specialization among organizational and social psychologists. The field is accelerating as archived virtual meetings provide vast swaths of data. And it is providing a fascinating window into human behavior.

Meeting to talk helps fulfill basic human needs to connect, communicate, and cooperate. People have long come together—in caves, fields, market squares, and town halls—to get something done, share ideas, get on the same page, or just to remark on the weather. But meeting scientists define their subject as gatherings of people “with some goal or structure to the event,” says organizational psychologist Liana Kreamer of the Florida Institute of Technology, who coauthored a review of over three decades of meeting science in the 2026 Annual Review of Organizational Psychology and Organizational Behavior.

As a graduate student, Kreamer was interested in studying teamwork, leadership, and work relationships. During her doctorate work with meeting scientist Steven Rogelberg, she realized that meetings would be a fine venue for studying all of that and more. “You can use a meeting as a stage to study anything you want,” she says. After all, at their core “meetings are a fundamental aspect of how we organize and interact as social beings,” Kreamer and coauthors Rogelberg and Jon Gray, both of the University of North Carolina in Charlotte, wrote in the 2026 article.

articles.headline: Zelenskyy says Trump is ‘rewarding Putin’ as he suspends Russia sanctions
keyFacts: President Donald Trump waived new bipartisan sanctions against Russia passed by Congress, citing national interest.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated that lifting the sanctions was wrong and effectively rewarded Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Several members of Congress from both parties also condemned the suspension of the sanctions.
body: President Donald Trump waived sweeping new sanctions against Russia passed by Congress, arguing in an executive order Friday that the move “is in the national interests of the United States.”

Trump had signed the legislation, named for the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C., just last month. The bill took aim at Russia’s largest buyers of oil and gas, allowing the president to impose tariffs on goods from those countries, which may include China and India.

Passed with bipartisan support, the bill was intended to target Russia’s revenue streams as the country continues to wage its war against Ukraine. Suspending the sanctions provides Russia a financial lifeline.

Trump’s decision to put a hold on the sanctions package comes after he announced a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin last week to release hundreds of thousands of tons of Russian diesel fuel onto the global market as fuel prices soar.

Trump has expressed frustration with Ukraine’s attacks on Russian oil and gas infrastructure and has blamed them for the increase in fuel costs while downplaying the impact of the Iran war on the oil market.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Saturday that lifting sanctions was “wrong” and “only helps the Russians.”

In a Telegram post, he decried what he called an “American sanctions blackout,” adding that a “weakening of pressure on the aggressor, effectively serving as a financial reward for Putin—only encourages him to continue his attacks.”
“It seems to me that this won’t stop Putin,” he later told journalists in WhatsApp messages. “On the contrary, he feels joy and happiness that there is such support.”
The decision to waive the Russia sanctions drew swift condemnation from critics in Congress.
Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., called the move a “craven, cowardly action” in a statement.
“These waivers have nothing to do with our national security, and everything to do with sucking up to Vladimir Putin,” Blumenthal said.

“Beyond irresponsible,” Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., who is retiring at the end of his term, wrote on X. “What part of enforcing a law passed 86-11 by the Senate does the President and his advisors not understand?”
“If the President wants to actually bring down energy prices, he can do it by solving the Iran problem, not by doing a solid for Vladimir Putin,” he added.
Rep. Don Bacon, R-Neb., a staunch Ukraine ally who is also not seeking re-election next month, said “the president is prolonging the war, not ending it,” in a post on X.
“Lindsey would be appalled,” Sen. John Cornyn, R-TX, who lost a primary to a Trump-backed challenger earlier this year, wrote.
Zelenskyy thanked both Democrats and Republicans who supported the legislation, and praised the late Graham for his prolonged vocal support for Ukraine.

“He always supported us very strongly and pushed for as much assistance to Ukraine as possible. It’s difficult without him, I’ll say frankly,” Zelenskyy said. “And I am grateful to his friends who supported him.”

Trump’s move to pause the sanctions comes as the price of diesel fuel has shot up almost 70% since the war in Iran began in February and comes less than three weeks before the midterm elections, as cost of living remains a top issue for voters.

Sen. Darline Graham, R-S.C., who co-sponsored the bill named for her late brother, has touted its success as a key part of her campaign to win a full term in his Senate seat. Graham is a fierce Trump ally, as his endorsement was critical in her GOP primary win. Graham has yet to criticize the president for his Russian oil deal or the decision to halt the sanctions.
Congress passed the legislation with strong majorities in both the House and Senate, though many Democrats opposed the bill because it granted the president new tariff powers.

The legislation states that before the administration waives the new sanctions, it must submit an unclassified report to Congress explaining its basis. In his executive order, Trump said the White House has sent the report to Capitol Hill.
